EMERALD CHAMPIONS — MASTER BATTLE DESIGN
VERSION: 2
AUTHORING_STATUS: Exact loadouts and plans are authored in emerald_champions_battle_teams.txt; this file materializes them. The Game Book is the short design guide.
REGENERATION_RULE: Run emerald_champions_teams.py --write to materialize the team catalogue; --check verifies source agreement. IDs remain stable.
CHRONOLOGY_RULE: Current map geometry, scripts and flags determine reachability; the Game Book battle/access section records the reconciled early-access ledger. campaign_order, atlas_ordinal, chapter and strict_cap are inherited authoring/preview metadata, not runtime gates or proof of first access. Use current book milestones and live-cap offsets for encounter levels.

SCOPE
source_checkpoint: modern Pokemon Champions migration branch
rematch_free_physical_encounter_groups: 324
rematch_free_explicit_trainer_branch_blocks: 368
format_counts: derived from active branch records; retired encounter IDs remain reserved
doubles_policy: every campaign trainer battle is double or multi; the opening rival has four Pokemon and all standard opposing teams have at least four
excluded_content: ordinary Match Call tiers, Gym rematch families, and three phantom source-parser hits
included_content: 324 active authored encounter groups; excluded branches remain retired
battle_frontier_boundary: every live Frontier challenge desk enters the single endless Champions Circuit, generated in-ROM from the pinned Showdown Champions random-doubles port; the retired native facility generators are not campaign encounters

DESIGN THESIS
Every campaign battle is a bespoke, legal, readable puzzle. The player receives competitive Pokemon, moves, abilities, natures, EVs, and free ordinary held items; difficulty comes from decisions rather than grinding.
All campaign trainers use the live chapter cap plus their authored offset on Normal; Hard adds 2 and Easy subtracts 2, represented in the native 1..255 battle-level range; no level-100 opponent ceiling. Gyms and the opening doubles are included. Teams and expert AI stay identical across difficulty settings.
Mega Evolution is the only selectable gimmick. Player Mega access begins with Steven's post-Brawly bracelet/Aerodactylite handoff. Roxanne's explicitly authored Mega Aerodactyl is the earlier opponent-only introduction. Primals remain approved automatic forms.

STATIC SOURCE AUDIT — NOT FULL PLAYTEST ACCEPTANCE
champions_legality_repairs: 584 move slots normalized against Showdown bb179fbf8449e3c31632bd56f671ffb4404fa6e7
coverage: all 99 Mega Stone item types occur in retained parties; legendary-family coverage is 73/78 under the current explicit alias index, not blanket acquisition/showcase acceptance
cohesion_contract: exact authored/native materialization, live-cap levels, valid native moves/forms/abilities/items and 510/252 EVs; roster-pattern and reference comparisons are advisory, not design quotas.

REMATCH POLICY
Ordinary and Gym rematches are not campaign content. League replays reuse the finished League teams. Gabby and Ty remain only as distinct roaming reporter milestones. Repeatable endgame variety belongs to the live Champions Circuit reached from every Frontier challenge desk.

IMPLEMENTATION CONTRACT
Implement every retained branch exactly: format, cap-relative levels, species, item, ability, nature, EVs, moves, AI requirements, and native dialogue intent. Build coherent changes and verify their relevant source, native behavior and artifact identity. Static checks do not certify unplayed battles or full progression.

On the next turn, cash in with Extreme Speed rather than continue setting up. Alternate deployment: Hoothoot Tailwind plus Starly gives an immediate attacking mode without Belly Drum. Reserves & disruption: If Drum is unsafe, attack with Zigzagoon or move to the bird pair. Figy is compatible with Adamant; Unnerve, item suppression or removal can deny recovery. Rattled is an opponent-dependent bonus, not an activation plan. Counterplay & audit: Priority immunity/denial, Fake Out on the support, physical mitigation, berry denial or focused damage before Drum resolves. Turn two switches Spinarak when its locked support action no longer produces value. Alternate deployment: Fast control beside Karrablast creates stronger immediate offensive conversion. Reserves & disruption: Dewpider supplies the special Water lane when physical attacks are contained. Do not let a Choice-locked utility move become repeated empty turns. Re-evaluate both targets, turn order, protection, stat-loss immunity, Contrary and retaliatory abilities. Counterplay & audit: Ground immunity blocks Electroweb damage but does not inherently block String Shot. Taunt, Magic Bounce, Clear Amulet, White Herb, speed reversal and punishing switches offer counterplay. Disposition: RETAIN; String Shot replaces Toxic Thread for direct paired speed control, while the Scarf control-and-switch identity remains.

primary_question: Can the player beat this regular team (Stakataka, Golurk, Cacturne, Perrserker) on its own terms: First two useful turns: Stakataka chooses Trick Room or Wide Guard according to survival and the expected spread threat while Golurk attacks. Turn two uses the reversed order or keeps attacking when room would favor the player. Alternate deployment: Perrserker's Fake Out supports Stakataka's room turn and its Steely Spirit can boost a relevant Steel attack. Reserves & disruption: Cacturne is a Water-immune priority reserve. Steely Spirit does not amplify unrelated Rock/Ghost moves and must be active beside the relevant user. Counterplay & audit: Fighting/Ground pressure, Taunt, slower opposing teams and targeted attacks. Disposition: Keep; distinguish true Steel amplification from a generic teamwide damage bonus. Could this team be cooler? The concept is unusual and worth keeping - a Beast Boost Stakataka setting Trick Room behind Wide Guard, with Steely Spirit amplifying a real Steel attack rather than acting as a generic team buff - but it was broken in execution: all four members are Brave and every one carried a 31 Speed IV, so the room it sets was working against its own team. Zeroing those Speed IVs is the whole difference between a Trick Room team and four slow Pokemon that happen to have a Trick Room user. The moment to remember is Wide Guard blanking a spread attack on the exact turn the room goes up.

AI executability: TRICK_ROOM has a real setter, ALLY_COMBO has Telepathy plus the printed INSTRUCT tactics; both are backed. Could this team be cooler? It is now: the old version let Fake Out delete the room turn for free and had a Speed-invested Girafarig sitting in a Trick Room. Leading Armor Tail beside the setter turns Parker's room into a puzzle the player has to solve without priority, and the Telepathy Earthquake loop is the interaction to remember. Keeping the Girafarig/Farigiraf pair is deliberate - the gym shows both halves of one line doing opposite jobs - and the honest counterplay is Taunt, a second Trick Room, or simply killing Oranguru before Lickilicky lands its first Earthquake. Level offsets are individual: Girafarig +6 and Spinda +4 as fragile members, the evolved room core +2.
intentional_weakness: Taunt or Encore Oranguru before the room lands, or set your own Trick Room to cancel it. Armor Tail stops priority, not speed control - Icy Wind, Electroweb or a Tailwind of your own inverts the room's maths. Levitate, Flying typing or a switch denies the Instructed Earthquake, and Farigiraf's Assault Vest means it can never Protect a losing turn.

battle_class: gym
ai_profile: sharp
primary_question: Can the player beat this gym team (Drampa, Rufflet, Obstagoon, Dudunsparce, Bewear, Lopunny) on its own terms: Room concept - the price of power. Every member of Mary's six pays for its damage with a drawback: Hustle's misses, a Choice lock, a self-inflicted burn, Fluffy's doubled Fire damage, Berserk's requirement to be hurt first, and recoil. Mega Lopunny's Scrappy is the deliberate exception - the clean blade in a room full of costs. First two useful turns: Drampa fires the best Choice Specs option while Rufflet pressures or U-turns; Drampa's Berserk is reactive, so the opening attack is not pre-boosted and the AI must not plan as though it were. Turn two respects the lock and Hustle's 80% accuracy instead of assuming both attacks connect. Alternate deployment: Mega Lopunny's Fake Out buys Drampa a clean Specs turn and Scrappy means Ghost leads do not blank it. Reserves & disruption: Obstagoon converts its own Flame Orb into Guts Facade, Dudunsparce's Serene Grace Coil endgame doubles Body Slam paralysis and Rock Slide flinch, and Bewear's Fluffy halves every contact move aimed at it. AI executability: SETUP is backed by Coil; there is no weather, terrain or room flag claimed that the loadout cannot deliver. Could this team be cooler? Yes - and the change is exactly the member that had no price and no payoff. Silvally with a bare RKS System was a Normal-typed Multi-Attack and nothing else; Bewear replaces it with a rare, genuinely scary Normal/Fighting body whose ability is a double-edged trade (contact halved, Fire doubled), which is the room's whole thesis. The interaction to remember is Obstagoon's burn turning into a Guts Facade the same turn Lopunny's Fake Out denies the answer. Honest counterplay: Fairy and Fighting hit most of the room, Fire melts Bewear, Wide Guard is useless here but Rocky Helmet is excellent, and every Choice lock and Hustle miss is a free turn the player can bank. Level offsets are individual: Rufflet +6 as an Eviolite pre-evolution, Mega Lopunny -1, the rest +2.
theme_and_tempo: Room concept - the price of power. Every member of Mary's six pays for its damage with a drawback: Hustle's misses, a Choice lock, a self-inflicted burn, Fluffy's doubled Fire damage, Berserk's requirement to be hurt first, and recoil. Mega Lopunny's Scrappy is the deliberate exception - the clean blade in a room full of costs. First two useful turns: Drampa fires the best Choice Specs option while Rufflet pressures or U-turns; Drampa's Berserk is reactive, so the opening attack is not pre-boosted and the AI must not plan as though it were. Turn two respects the lock and Hustle's 80% accuracy instead of assuming both attacks connect. Alternate deployment: Mega Lopunny's Fake Out buys Drampa a clean Specs turn and Scrappy means Ghost leads do not blank it. Reserves & disruption: Obstagoon converts its own Flame Orb into Guts Facade, Dudunsparce's Serene Grace Coil endgame doubles Body Slam paralysis and Rock Slide flinch, and Bewear's Fluffy halves every contact move aimed at it. AI executability: SETUP is backed by Coil; there is no weather, terrain or room flag claimed that the loadout cannot deliver. Could this team be cooler? Yes - and the change is exactly the member that had no price and no payoff. Silvally with a bare RKS System was a Normal-typed Multi-Attack and nothing else; Bewear replaces it with a rare, genuinely scary Normal/Fighting body whose ability is a double-edged trade (contact halved, Fire doubled), which is the room's whole thesis. The interaction to remember is Obstagoon's burn turning into a Guts Facade the same turn Lopunny's Fake Out denies the answer. Level offsets are individual: Rufflet +6 as an Eviolite pre-evolution, Mega Lopunny -1, the rest +2.
intentional_weakness: Punish the drawbacks rather than out-damaging them. Stall a Hustle miss, Encore or Taunt the Choice user, use a Fire move on Bewear where Fluffy doubles it, and keep Drampa below the Berserk threshold or kill it through the threshold in one hit. Fairy/Fighting coverage and contact punishment handle the rest.

primary_question: Can the player beat this gym team (Zangoose, Ursaring, Linoone, Bibarel, Swellow, Ursaluna) on its own terms: Room concept - the berserkers, every one of whom poisons or burns itself on purpose. First two useful turns: Zangoose and Ursaring let their Orbs land at end of turn and attack or take one justified guard; the AI must not Protect a harmless slot while the partner is removed. Turn two runs on real Toxic Boost and Guts numbers, not anticipated ones - before the Orb activates these are ordinary attackers and should be played that way. Alternate deployment: Swellow's Toxic Orb Guts Facade is the fast third orb, giving Alexia an immediate-speed mode when the slower bears are a bad matchup; it also pivots with U-turn to bring a bear in safely. Reserves & disruption: Linoone takes a benchmarked Belly Drum only when Extreme Speed can actually close, Bibarel stacks Simple Curse (+2 Attack, +2 Defense per use) and now finishes with priority Aqua Jet, and Ursaluna's Bulletproof is the room's answer to Focus Blast, Sludge Bomb and Shadow Ball. AI executability: SETUP is backed by Belly Drum, Curse and Swords Dance. Stats/legality fixes applied: Bibarel's Superpower was actively anti-synergistic - Simple doubles the Attack and Defense drops as well as the Curse boosts - so it becomes Aqua Jet, which is what a slow +2 sweeper actually needs. Swellow replaces it with the Hoenn Guts icon and completes the thesis - three self-inflicted status conditions on one team, each converting a "bad" status into the room's best damage. The interaction to remember is a Toxic Orb ticking on turn one while the player is still deciding whether it was a mistake. Honest counterplay: burst them before the Orbs pay, deny priority, Taunt the setup and remember that a Guts or Toxic Boost attacker is on a clock its own poison is running. ai_profile: master
primary_question: Can the player beat this leader team (Weezing Galar, Slaking, Indeedee F, Porygon2, Meloetta, Staraptor) on its own terms: Leader concept - Norman answers his own gym's thesis. Six rooms have each shown a Normal-type paying a price for its power; Norman brings the Pokemon with the worst price in the game and simply switches it off. First two useful turns: Galarian Weezing's Neutralizing Gas suppresses every ability on the field, Truant included, so Choice Band Slaking attacks every single turn while Weezing burns or attacks a real threat. Turn two preserves the Gas only while it is actually protecting Slaking's output - if Weezing is about to die anyway, it should spend its last turn on damage or a burn rather than a pointless guard. Alternate deployment: once Weezing is gone, Indeedee-F and Meloetta form a completely different battle - Psychic Surge under a Terrain Extender turns Expanding Force into a spread attack and Follow Me protects the pair, and both the Surge and Porygon2's Download only come online because the Gas has left. Kept, and the lead is the reason: Munkidori's Toxic Chain gives every attack a 30% chance to badly poison on top of its damage, which turns Choice Specs Psychic into a spread-format clock rather than a single number, and Jynx's Lovely Kiss is 75%-accurate sleep with Dry Skin bulk behind a Focus Sash. Musharna and Chimecho are the support half - Light Screen, Thunder Wave, Helping Hand and Heal Pulse - so this is genuinely a psychic-support team rather than four attackers. The improvement worth naming is that Synchronize on Musharna wants the player to inflict status and nothing here makes that likely. Offsets individual: +1 across the evolved three, Chimecho +2 as the fragile support that has to survive to matter.

Could this team be cooler? primary_question: Can the player beat this grunt team (Pelipper, Ferrothorn, Inteleon, Ludicolo) on its own terms: Raid stage 4 - the machine room, and the first grunt who has actually turned something on. Pelipper's Drizzle is Aqua getting what it came for, and the rest of the raid escalates from here. First two useful turns: Pelipper establishes rain and chooses Tailwind, or Wide Guard when that is what protects Ferrothorn's turn; Ferrothorn attacks or takes a survivable Iron Defense behind Iron Barbs, which taxes every contact move aimed at it. Turn two converts Defense into Body Press, or abandons the slow plan for a special reserve if the rain matters more than the wall. Alternate deployment: Pelipper and Swift Swim Ludicolo are the straightforward fast-rain pressure mode, and under rain Ludicolo's Hydro Pump is the crew's biggest single number. Reserves & disruption: Inteleon's Snipe Shot ignores redirection entirely, which is the answer to a Follow Me or Rage Powder player, and Sniper multiplies a critical hit rather than guaranteeing one - without Focus Energy it is a chance, not a plan. Rain weakens Fire damage; it does not create immunity. AI executability: RAIN has an automatic setter, TAILWIND a real user, SETUP an Iron Defense; all three flags are backed. Could this team be cooler? The composition earns retention and the contrast is the point - a defensive Steel mode and a fast Water mode in one grunt, chosen against what the player leads, is more interesting than a fourth interchangeable rain sweeper, and the Snipe Shot answer to redirection is a genuinely uncommon tool at this stage. What it lacked was raid position: as the room where Aqua first seizes the weather it should read as a step up from the lobby, so its offsets move to +2. The moment to remember is Snipe Shot going straight through a Follow Me. Honest counterplay: replace the weather and Ludicolo, Pelipper and the Fire-resistance all weaken at once.

First two useful turns: Mightyena's Intimidate lands on entry and Howl raises the Attack of both Mightyena and its partner, which is what makes this a doubles support move rather than a selfish boost; Golisopod uses First Impression only on its genuine entry turn, because the move is dead from turn two onward. Turn two must account for Emergency Exit - if Golisopod drops below half it is pulled out whether Aqua wanted it or not, which can end a planned boosted attack before it happens. Alternate deployment: Alolan Muk and Qwilfish are the slower poison-control mode - Muk's Poison/Dark typing resists most of what a player brings to a Ghost-free room, and Qwilfish's second Intimidate stacks with Mightyena's. Reserves & disruption: Spikes and Curse should not both burn a turn in the same battle; one of them is the plan and the other is a concession. Sucker Punch fails against any non-attacking turn. AI executability: SETUP is backed by Howl and Curse. Could this team be cooler? The honest answer to "could it be cooler" is that its weakness was presentation, not species: a raid boss's antechamber was running the same flat offsets as the lobby. It now sits at +2 to +3, the highest of the grunts, and the moment to remember is deliberately damaging Golisopod to force it out of a winning position. physical_group_id: PHYSICAL_ROUTE119_WEATHERINSTITUTE_2F_0051

campaign_order: 248
atlas_ordinal: 248
chapter: Feather Badge
strict_cap: 55
location: Route119_WeatherInstitute_2F
requirement: required
status: master_audited_ready_for_implementation
battle_class: admin
ai_profile: master
primary_question: Can the player beat this admin team (Ninetales Alola, Empoleon, Clefable, Castform, Rotom Wash, Feraligatr) on its own terms: Raid boss - Shelly does not steal the weather machine, she reprograms it. Five grunts escalate from no weather, to a stolen rain switch, and then the admin turns the whole Institute to snow and fights the player inside a building that is now working for Aqua. That is the reason this boss is not a second rain team, and it is also why two of her six are the Institute's own Pokemon, commandeered rather than caught. First two useful turns: Alolan Ninetales sets Snow Warning on entry and takes Aurora Veil behind Light Clay - eight turns of halved damage on both sides is the single biggest number in the fight - while Empoleon applies Hydro Pump/Flash Cannon pressure and punishes only genuine opposing stat drops through Competitive. Turn two exploits the Veil: Clefable's Follow Me absorbs a double-target so Mega Feraligatr can Dragon Dance safely, and Sheer Force Liquidation and Ice Punch lose their secondary effects but gain 1.3x damage in exchange. Alternate deployment: Castform beside Ninetales is the Institute's own research Pokemon turned against its keepers - under Shelly's snow Forecast makes Castform an Ice type, so Weather Ball is a 100-power same-type attack and Blizzard never misses; it is the thematic heart of the fight. Reserves & disruption: Rotom-Wash is the Levitate Electric pivot, and Clefable's Unaware means a player who answered the grunts by setting up finds those boosts simply ignored. AI executability: SNOW has an automatic setter, REDIRECTION a real Follow Me user, SETUP a real Dragon Dance; the custom Mega Feraligatr transition remains a source and native gate to confirm. Could this team be cooler? Yes, and one slot was quietly dead: Kingdra's Damp does nothing outside Explosion and Aftermath, so the boss was carrying a 540-BST body with a blank ability and a generic special kit. Castform replaces it with the one Pokemon that belongs in this building more than any other, and its ability is not flavour - Forecast is the mechanic that ties the boss to the room she is standing in. Clefable is likewise re-read as the Institute's own, which resolves the only other thematic loose end. The moment to remember is a Castform turning white as Shelly's snow lands and immediately throwing a perfect-accuracy Blizzard. Honest counterplay: take the weather back and four of her six get worse at once. Level offsets are individual and boss-grade: Castform +5 because it is a frail 420-BST body carrying a key role, Mega Feraligatr +3, the support core +3 to +4.

battle_class: rival
ai_profile: master
primary_question: Can the player beat this rival team (Swellow, Manectric, Breloom, Shiftry, Mimikyu, Sceptile) on its own terms: Rival concept - the Hoenn team the player could have built, assembled better. All six branch aliases are one design: the first five slots are fixed and only the fourth member and the ace change, so the rival always covers the starter the player chose and always leads the same way. First two useful turns: Swellow's Flame Orb lands at the end of turn one and from turn two its Guts Facade is a 140-power attack from a burned body that can no longer be burned again, while Manectric decides between Thunderbolt pressure and a Volt Switch pivot - Lightning Rod is the reason this pair can stand together at all, because it draws the Electric attacks that would otherwise delete Swellow. Turn two exploits whatever the Orb and the pivot bought; before the burn lands Swellow is an ordinary bird and must be played as one. Alternate deployment: Breloom's Toxic Orb Poison Heal is the second, opposite orb - the same self-inflicted status converted into recovery instead of damage - and a 100%-accurate Spore plus priority Mach Punch is the disruption mode when the bird lead is a bad matchup. Reserves & disruption: the branch-specific fourth member exists to threaten the regional starter the player did NOT pick (Shiftry and Sceptile against a Mudkip player, Ludicolo and Swampert against Torchic, Camerupt and Blaziken against Treecko), and Mimikyu's Disguise guarantees it one free turn for Will-O-Wisp or Taunt while Mental Herb covers a Taunt of the player's own. Shiftry's Pickpocket cannot trigger while it still holds its Sitrus Berry - it comes online only after the berry is eaten, which is a sequencing note rather than a dead ability. AI executability: no strategy flag is claimed and none is backed; this is a disruption-and-orbs team, not a weather or room team, and Ace Pokemon correctly points the AI at the starter. Could this team be cooler? The composition earns retention and should not be churned: two orbs paying off in opposite directions, a redirection ability protecting the member that needs it, guaranteed sleep, a guaranteed free turn, and a starter that always answers the player's own - that is a genuinely tight six-slot Hoenn design and it reads instantly as a rival rather than a route trainer. The one change worth considering later is giving the ace a Mega stone so the rival escalates visibly across the campaign; it is deferred here because Blazikenite and Sceptilite both already have homes earlier in the game and duplicating them at Route 119 would flatten those showcases. The moment to remember is Lightning Rod eating a Thunderbolt aimed at a burned Swellow that then hits back for 140. What did need fixing was the levels: a blanket zero made the campaign's mid-game rival the same difficulty as the regulars around it. Every member goes to +2 and the ace to +4. Counterplay & audit: powder immunity, priority, Ground pressure and denying repeated pivots.

primary_question: Can the player beat this regular team (Ninetales, Weepinbell, Ninetales Alola, Torterra) on its own terms: First two useful turns: Ninetales establishes sun while Weepinbell attacks or uses a legal Sleep Powder; turn two exploits Chlorophyll before considering a switch. Alternate deployment: Alolan Ninetales and Torterra form the separate snow/Veil matchup mode. Reserves & disruption: Switching to Alolan Ninetales replaces sun and removes Weepinbell's Chlorophyll advantage. Veil is not an additional benefit layered on permanent sun. Counterplay & audit: Weather control, Taunt, Fire/Flying pressure and exploiting the setter switch. Disposition: Keep as a genuine two-weather puzzle only with explicit mutually exclusive modes and a reason to change them. Could this team be cooler? It is kept exactly because of what looks like a bug: two sisters, two Ninetales, two incompatible weathers. Kantonian Ninetales's Drought and Alolan Ninetales's Snow Warning overwrite each other, and the deployment order is the design - the lead pair is sun (Drought plus Chlorophyll Weepinbell), and the Alolan half with Aurora Veil is the second mode after the first falls. The player therefore fights the same trainer under two different skies, and the memorable moment is the weather flipping when the second sister's Ninetales comes out. Torterra's Solid Rock is the grounded body that does not care either way. The honest caution is that the AI must never send both Ninetales out together, which would waste one of them. Offsets individual: the Eviolite Weepinbell at +1, the rest low.

primary_question: Can the player beat this gym team (Honchkrow, Jumpluff, Vespiquen, Mandibuzz, Toucannon, Braviary) on its own terms: Room concept - the carrion flock: nothing here fights fair. First two useful turns: Jumpluff is now a dedicated support - Rage Powder pulls both player attacks onto a Focus Sash body while Honchkrow takes a free Brave Bird or Sucker Punch, and Sleep Powder or Encore replaces the redirection turn when the player has a powder-immune lead. Turn two is the Moxie turn: a single knockout behind redirection snowballs Honchkrow's Attack, and Life Orb Brave Bird from +1 is what actually ends the room. Alternate deployment: Mandibuzz Tailwind supporting Choice Band Braviary is the honest plan when sleep and powder are off the table entirely - Overcoat also means Mandibuzz never eats an opposing Spore. Reserves & disruption: Vespiquen is the Defend Order pivot that heals the pair, and Skill Link Toucannon breaks Focus Sash and Substitute with Bullet Seed and Rock Blast while Beak Blast punishes contact. Defiant on Braviary triggers on opposing stat drops only - friendly Intimidate or a self-inflicted drop must never be credited. AI executability: TAILWIND has a real user; REDIRECTION is now genuinely backed by Rage Powder rather than implied by the theme. Could this team be cooler? Yes, and the fix is small and exact: Jumpluff was carrying Acrobatics, a fourth mediocre attack on a Pokemon with 55 Attack, in a room whose whole win condition is giving Honchkrow one safe turn. Rage Powder converts it into the enabler the Moxie plan needs, and the interaction to remember is a Focus Sash Jumpluff eating a double-target so a Life Orb Honchkrow can start snowballing. Honest counterplay: powder immunity (Grass types, Overcoat, Safety Goggles) blanks both of Jumpluff's key moves at once, Rock and Electric punish the whole flock, and Sucker Punch fails against any non-attacking turn. Level offsets are individual and flat at +2 across an evolved, well-rounded six - nothing here is a fragile pre-evolution needing compensation.

First two useful turns: Yanmega attacks or takes a Speed Boost turn behind Focus Sash while Archeops fires Earthquake beside it - both of Flint's leads are airborne, so the spread Ground move hits only the player's side. Turn two rechecks the state rather than the species list: a Roost, a Gravity, an Ingrain or an ability suppression grounds the partner and the same Earthquake becomes a mistake. Alternate deployment: Choice Scarf Flygon and Mega Salamence are the fastest version of the same idea, Levitate and Aerilate respectively, with Salamence's Double-Edge converting to Flying. Reserves & disruption: Tropius is the Harvest/Sitrus recovery body that keeps recycling its berry and draining with Leech Seed, and Dragonite is the Multiscale Dragon Dance option - note that Dragonite is grounded, so it is the one member that must never be on the field for an ally Earthquake. Archeops deliberately carries no item so its Acrobatics is at full 110 power, and its Defeatist is the honest price. AI executability: ALLY_COMBO is backed by a real, mechanical airborne-Earthquake relationship rather than a flavour claim, and SETUP by Dragon Dance. Could this team be cooler? This is already the best-conceived room in the gym and it keeps its composition - the itemless Acrobatics Archeops is a genuinely clever build and the Ground/Flying spread engine is the most distinctive thing in Fortree. What it lacked was individual levels: a blanket zero offset made a room with two legend-tier Dragons read the same as the filler rooms. The interaction to remember is a spread Earthquake that the player's team eats twice while Flint's pair floats above it. Honest counterplay: Ice and Rock hit almost everything, Wide Guard blanks both Earthquake and Rock Slide, and grounding effects turn the room's engine against itself.

primary_question: Can the player beat this gym team (Pelipper, Gyarados, Mantine, Cramorant, Swanna, Pidgeot) on its own terms: Room concept - the storm room, and the only one in Fortree where the sky is wet. First two useful turns: Pelipper's Drizzle lands on entry and it chooses between Tailwind and immediate Hurricane/Muddy Water pressure - under its own rain Hurricane never misses, which is the reason this room exists. Gyarados leads beside it, drops Intimidate on both player slots and either attacks or takes one Dragon Dance behind Lum Berry. Turn two converts: Mantine's Swift Swim comes online, Swanna's Hydration scrubs any status at end of turn and its Weather Ball is a 100-power Water move, and Cramorant's Surf is now safe to fire because every partner on the field resists Water. Alternate deployment: Pelipper and Mantine are the bulky special rain pair when the player's lead punishes physical setup. Reserves & disruption: Mega Pidgeot's No Guard-grade Hurricane accuracy is redundant in rain but its Heat Wave is actively weakened by it - the AI must not pick the Fire option under its own weather. Gulp Missile fires only on Surf or Dive and retaliates against whoever damaged Cramorant afterwards. AI executability: RAIN has an automatic setter, TAILWIND a real user, SETUP now has a genuine Dragon Dance rather than a Swords Dance that had nothing to do with the weather. Could this team be cooler? Yes, and the change fixes a real defect rather than adding a bigger name. Ninjask was a sun-and-sand-agnostic Swords Dance bug in a rain room, and worse, it was grounded and Water-neutral, so Cramorant's Surf hit its own partner. Gyarados is Water/Flying: it resists the friendly Surf, it wants the rain, Intimidate supports a fragile flock, and Dragon Dance gives the room a physical win condition it did not have. The interaction to remember is Gulp Missile spitting an Arrokuda back into the face of whoever just knocked Cramorant's health down. Honest counterplay: replace the weather, or bring Electric - the whole room is five Water/Flying-adjacent bodies. Level offsets are individual: Mega Pidgeot -1, Gyarados +1 because Intimidate plus Dragon Dance is already a tier, the rest +2.

primary_question: Can the player beat this gym team (Gliscor, Corviknight, Rotom Fan, Shedinja, Hawlucha, Sigilyph) on its own terms: Room concept - six Pokemon that refuse to pay the usual price. Poison Heal turns poison into recovery, Magic Guard turns Life Orb recoil into nothing, Mirror Armor returns stat drops to the sender, Unburden turns a consumed item into doubled Speed, Levitate ignores the ground, and Wonder Guard ignores almost everything. First two useful turns: Gliscor lets its Toxic Orb land - after that it is healing 12.5% a turn - and either attacks or takes a Swords Dance beside Corviknight, whose Mirror Armor punishes an Intimidate or Icy Wind lead by sending the drop straight back. Turn two accounts for the real state: Roost grounds Corviknight for the turn, and Poison Heal only exists after the Orb has actually activated. Alternate deployment: Hawlucha's White Herb is the room's cleverest line - Close Combat's own Defense drops consume the Herb, which triggers Unburden, which doubles its Speed; Sigilyph is the special counterpart, taking Life Orb recoil for free through Magic Guard. Reserves & disruption: Rotom-Fan is the Levitate pivot with Will-O-Wisp, and Shedinja is the room's thesis taken to its limit - a Safety Goggles body that only Rock, Fire, Flying, Ghost and Dark can touch at all, and Safety Goggles is specifically there because powder and weather chip are the honest ways to kill it. AI executability: SETUP is backed by two Swords Dances; nothing claims a weather or terrain the room cannot make. Could this team be cooler? Yes, and it required removing a duplicate rather than adding a name. Humberto's Choice Scarf Archeops was the same species Flint fields two rooms earlier in the same gym, which is the clearest overrepresentation defect in Fortree. Shedinja replaces it and completes the room's identity perfectly - it is the ultimate drawback-denial Pokemon, it is Hoenn-native, and it turns one slot of six into a puzzle the player must actually answer rather than out-damage. The moment to remember is a 1 HP Bug/Ghost walling an entire turn while Gliscor heals through its own poison beside it. Honest counterplay: every one of these abilities has a named answer, and a player who brings two of them wins. First two useful turns: Tornadus uses Prankster Tailwind before the player's fastest Pokemon can Taunt it, and that Tailwind is a wind move - Kilowattrel's Wind Power reads it and comes out of the turn Charged, so its next Thunderbolt is doubled. Turn two spends the charge and the speed together rather than re-setting Tailwind; Taunt is the alternative opening when the player's lead is a setter rather than an attacker. Alternate deployment: Tornadus supporting Mega Aerodactyl is the physical mode - Rock Slide and Earthquake under Tailwind from a body that outspeeds essentially everything at this stage. Reserves & disruption: Choice Specs Sheer Force Braviary-Hisui is the immediate special breaker, Togekiss is Serene Grace speed control and spread Fairy damage, and Unfezant is the crit lane - Super Luck plus Scope Lens plus Focus Energy reaches a guaranteed critical hit, which ignores the player's Intimidate, Reflect and Defense boosts entirely. Hurricane is inaccurate without rain and nothing here makes rain; do not grant it accuracy because Tornadus is present. AI executability: TAILWIND has a Prankster user, and ALLY_COMBO is now backed by the printed ACTIVATE tactic rather than being decorative. Could this team be cooler? Yes on two counts, both of which were real defects. Tropius was a straight duplicate of Flint's Tropius - identical species, item, ability, nature, spread and moves, two rooms apart inside one gym - and Unfezant was a third interchangeable Brave Bird body. Kilowattrel converts the room's own Tailwind into a damage buff, which is the single most thematic engine available to a wind room, and the Focus Energy Unfezant becomes the answer to a player who tries to wall Darius with stat boosts. The moment to remember is a priority Tailwind that simultaneously buffs the team's Speed and charges a partner's next attack. Honest counterplay: Taunt, Prankster-blocking Dark types, and simply outlasting eight Tailwind turns. Level offsets are individual: Tornadus +0 because it is a legendary already above its weight class here, Mega Aerodactyl -1, Unfezant +3 to make the crit lane genuinely threatening, the rest +2.

Turn two spends the charge and the speed together rather than re-setting Tailwind; Taunt is the alternative opening when the player's lead is a setter rather than an attacker. Alternate deployment: Tornadus supporting Mega Aerodactyl is the physical mode - Rock Slide and Earthquake under Tailwind from a body that outspeeds essentially everything at this stage. Reserves & disruption: Choice Specs Sheer Force Braviary-Hisui is the immediate special breaker, Togekiss is Serene Grace speed control and spread Fairy damage, and Unfezant is the crit lane - Super Luck plus Scope Lens plus Focus Energy reaches a guaranteed critical hit, which ignores the player's Intimidate, Reflect and Defense boosts entirely. Hurricane is inaccurate without rain and nothing here makes rain; do not grant it accuracy because Tornadus is present. The moment to remember is a priority Tailwind that simultaneously buffs the team's Speed and charges a partner's next attack. Honest counterplay: Taunt, Prankster-blocking Dark types, and simply outlasting eight Tailwind turns. primary_question: Can the player beat this leader team (Zapdos, Altaria, Enamorus, Talonflame, Noivern, Skarmory) on its own terms: Leader concept - the whole sky, not one weather. Each of Winona's rooms showed the player a single trick; she brings two legendaries, a custom Mega and three of the best support tools in the type, and no two of her members are answered the same way. First two useful turns: Zapdos applies immediate Thunderbolt/Hurricane pressure while Altaria decides between Tailwind and Haze - Haze is the new and important option, because it erases a player's Dragon Dance, Calm Mind or Belly Drum on the turn it was supposed to pay off, and Natural Cure means Altaria can cycle a status off by switching. Turn two brings Enamorus into the matchup it wants: Contrary means Superpower raises its Attack instead of dropping it, so repeated Superpowers get stronger, and the AI must treat that as a growth curve rather than a one-shot. Alternate deployment: Gale Wings Talonflame gives priority Brave Bird from full health regardless of Tailwind, which is the answer when the player wins the speed war outright; Choice Specs Noivern with Infiltrator ignores screens and Substitutes. Reserves & disruption: Mega Skarmory is a separate endgame rather than a seventh attacker - Iron Defense into Body Press wins a long game that Winona's fast half cannot. AI executability: TAILWIND and SETUP both have real users; Ace Pokemon is correct for a team whose plan pivots on Enamorus. Could this team be cooler? The composition earns retention and the Mega register confirms it should keep it - Skarmorite has no other home in the campaign, so moving the stone to Altaria would orphan a custom Mega. What was genuinely weak was Altaria itself: four slots of Dragon Pulse, Roost, Helping Hand and Tailwind made the leader's signature Pokemon the least threatening thing on the field and gave her six broadly interchangeable attacking turns. Haze replaces Dragon Pulse so Altaria is the reason a player's setup plan fails, which is a much more memorable role for her ace than a resisted Dragon attack. Honest counterplay: Rock and Ice hit almost everything, but Skarmory laughs at both and needs special Fire or Electric instead - Winona is deliberately not solvable with one coverage move. Level offsets are individual and a clear step beyond the +2 gym rooms: Altaria, Talonflame and Noivern +3, Zapdos and Enamorus +2 as already-strong legendaries, Mega Skarmory +1.

Kept, and it is deliberately the broadest coverage six in the stretch: Sheer Force Feraligatr trading secondary effects for 1.3x damage, Motor Drive Electivire turning an Electric attack into a Speed boost, Mega Sceptile as the special Grass/Dragon lane, and Tough Claws Lycanroc-Dusk with Accelerock for priority. Reckless Bouffalant behind a Clear Amulet cannot be Intimidated out of Head Charge. The honest weakness is the same as most six-attacker teams - no support turn, no speed control, no way to buy a setup - so Pat is a wall of good individual builds rather than a plan. Flagged rather than rebuilt, because the coverage itself is what makes the fight hard. Offsets individual and flat at +1 with Lycanroc-Dusk at +2 as the priority closer.

primary_question: Can the player beat this rival team (Swellow, Manectric, Breloom, Hariyama, Salamence, Sceptile) on its own terms: The Lilycove rival is one design in six printings: five fixed members that are the rival's actual team, plus the starter that beats the player's. First two useful turns: Swellow's Flame Orb activates at the end of turn one and Guts then raises its Attack by 50 percent while the burn cannot reduce it, because Facade doubles against a statused user - so the rival's opening is to survive one turn and then hit with a 140 base power attack. Manectric's Lightning Rod draws every Electric attack on the field to itself and converts it into +1 Special Attack, and Volt Switch keeps the rival's positioning ahead of the player's. Alternate deployment: Breloom's Toxic Orb plus Poison Heal makes it immune to further status while healing an eighth per turn, and Spore is the most reliable disruption in the game; Hariyama's Thick Fat halves the Fire and Ice attacks aimed at the rival's Grass and Flying members and Fake Out buys the Mega turn. Reserves & disruption: Mega Salamence is the rival's constant ace in every variant - Aerilate turns Double-Edge into a Flying attack with a 20 percent boost, and Dragon Dance behind Intimidate makes it the win condition. The sixth slot is the starter chosen to beat the player's, and it is the only thing that changes between the six branches. Counterplay & audit: Grass and powder immunity, Electric immunity or a non-Electric answer to Manectric, Fairy and Ice pressure on Salamence, and denying the free Dragon Dance turn. Could this team be cooler? The old six branches differed in both the starter and the Mega, which meant the rival had three different aces and no identity at all - and two of those Megas, Metagross and Tyranitar, now belong to Magma's Space Center raid and its hideout gate. It is cooler now because the rival is a person the player can learn: the same five Pokemon, the same Guts-and-Poison-Heal status engine, the same Mega Salamence, and one slot that says "I picked the one that beats yours". That is a rival, rather than a randomiser.

First two useful turns: Swellow's Flame Orb activates at the end of turn one and Guts then raises its Attack by 50 percent while the burn cannot reduce it, because Facade doubles against a statused user - so the rival's opening is to survive one turn and then hit with a 140 base power attack. Manectric's Lightning Rod draws every Electric attack on the field to itself and converts it into +1 Special Attack, and Volt Switch keeps the rival's positioning ahead of the player's. Alternate deployment: Breloom's Toxic Orb plus Poison Heal makes it immune to further status while healing an eighth per turn, and Spore is the most reliable disruption in the game; Hariyama's Thick Fat halves the Fire and Ice attacks aimed at the rival's Grass and Flying members and Fake Out buys the Mega turn. Reserves & disruption: Mega Salamence is the rival's constant ace in every variant - Aerilate turns Double-Edge into a Flying attack with a 20 percent boost, and Dragon Dance behind Intimidate makes it the win condition. The sixth slot is the starter chosen to beat the player's, and it is the only thing that changes between the six branches. Counterplay & audit: Grass and powder immunity, Electric immunity or a non-Electric answer to Manectric, Fairy and Ice pressure on Salamence, and denying the free Dragon Dance turn. Could this team be cooler? The old six branches differed in both the starter and the Mega, which meant the rival had three different aces and no identity at all - and two of those Megas, Metagross and Tyranitar, now belong to Magma's Space Center raid and its hideout gate. It is cooler now because the rival is a person the player can learn: the same five Pokemon, the same Guts-and-Poison-Heal status engine, the same Mega Salamence, and one slot that says "I picked the one that beats yours". That is a rival, rather than a randomiser.
intentional_weakness: Grass typing or Safety Goggles beats Spore; do not aim Electric attacks at Manectric; Fairy, Ice and Rock pressure on Salamence; Fake Out and priority deny the Dragon Dance turn; the Flame and Toxic Orbs are Knock Off targets on turn one.
first_loss_lesson: Grass typing or Safety Goggles beats Spore; do not aim Electric attacks at Manectric; Fairy, Ice and Rock pressure on Salamence; Fake Out and priority deny the Dragon Dance turn; the Flame and Toxic Orbs are Knock Off targets on turn one.

Alternate deployment: Mega Milotic with Competitive is the redirection payoff - behind Follow Me it takes a turn it would not otherwise get, and any stat drop aimed at it returns +2 Special Attack. Reserves & disruption: Haxorus takes Swords Dance behind Follow Me and Klinklang takes Shift Gear behind it; Togekiss' Serene Grace doubles Air Slash's flinch chance to 60 percent, which is a second, less honest form of turn denial. Volcarona is the Quiver Dance win condition if the physical lane is answered. Counterplay & audit: spread moves ignore Follow Me entirely and are the correct answer, Taunt stops the redirection, and Electric and Grass pressure removes Milotic. Could this team be cooler? Asked honestly, no - Buffel is a route ace whose team is a clean, complete statement of one doubles principle: buy a turn, protect the turn, spend the turn. Every member either creates a free turn or uses one. The audit's only note is that this trainer teaches Follow Me shortly before a Psychic gym that punishes redirection habits with Armor Tail and Stalwart, which is good campaign structure rather than a defect.

ai_profile: sharp
primary_question: Can the player beat this ace team (Abomasnow, Sandslash Alola, Cetitan, Frosmoth, Avalugg, Mamoswine) on its own terms: First two useful turns: Mega Abomasnow's Snow Warning is automatic and snow raises the Defense of every Ice type on the field by 50 percent, so Gabrielle's whole team becomes physically bulkier the moment the battle starts. Alolan Sandslash's Slush Rush doubles its Speed in that snow and Cetitan's does the same, so the team has two sweepers running off one weather. Alternate deployment: Frosmoth's Ice Scales halves every special attack it takes, which is the answer to the Fire and Rock special coverage a player brings to an Ice team, and Quiver Dance behind that makes it the win condition. Reserves & disruption: Avalugg's Sturdy guarantees one survived hit and Body Press converts its 184 base Defense - already raised by snow - into damage; Mamoswine's Thick Fat halves the Fire and Ice attacks aimed at it and Ice Shard is the priority finish. Counterplay & audit: replace the weather and both Slush Rush sweepers halve, Fire and Fighting and Rock and Steel all bite, and Frosmoth folds instantly to physical damage. Could this team be cooler? The old build was flagged RAIN and SNOW at once and actually ran both - a Gorebyss using Rain Dance beside a Snow Warning Abomasnow, so the two engines deleted each other every time either resolved. That is a genuine strategic defect, not a flavour note. It is cooler now because it is one committed weather with two Slush Rush abusers, an Ice Scales special wall and a Body Press physical wall, and because Frosmoth and Cetitan are both first appearances in the campaign. Asked again after the revision: the team now has a real reason to be an ace-class fight instead of a pile of cold Pokemon.

primary_question: Can the player beat this grunt team (Liepard, Raticate Alola, Qwilfish Hisui, Lanturn) on its own terms: Mt Pyre is an away mission, not a hideout - Aqua has sent a light scouting party up a graveyard mountain, so this group is deliberately the thinnest crew in the faction and reads that way. First two useful turns: Liepard's Prankster gives priority Fake Out-free disruption; Encore locks a player who spent turn one on setup or Protect, and Taunt denies the support the player needs, with Foul Play as the damage that uses the player's own Attack stat. Alolan Raticate's Hustle trades accuracy for a 50 percent Attack boost, so its Double-Edge is a real threat that sometimes simply misses. Alternate deployment: Hisuian Qwilfish brings Intimidate on entry and Barb Barrage doubles in power against a poisoned target, so Toxic Spikes-free poison from its own attacks compounds. Reserves & disruption: Lanturn's Volt Absorb makes the Electric attack the player packed for a Water crew into a heal. Counterplay & audit: Fighting and Fairy pressure, Safety Goggles are irrelevant here, and Prankster is stopped by Dark typing. Could this team be cooler? The old block was Muk, Alolan Raticate, Tentacruel and Mightyena - three of which now belong to the Magma Hideout or the Aqua bilge watch, so the mountain shared a wardrobe with everything else. It is cooler now because the scouting party has its own look: a thief cat, a plague rat, a Hisuian pufferfish and a deep-sea lantern, none of which appear anywhere else in the campaign. The room's memorable moment is Encore turning the player's own Protect into a wasted second turn.

physical_group_id: PHYSICAL_MTPYRE_SUMMIT_0604

ai_profile: sharp
primary_question: Can the player beat this grunt team (Polteageist Antique, Weavile, Mismagius, Carracosta) on its own terms: The grave robbers, working the tomb floors. First two useful turns: Weavile's Fake Out buys the turn and Antique Polteageist spends it on Shell Smash - +2 Special Attack, +2 Special Defense-free, +2 Speed - with a White Herb restoring the defence drops immediately, so the crew converts one bought turn into a genuine sweeper. Mismagius' Levitate keeps it above the Ground attacks the player brought for the earlier Poison crew. Alternate deployment: if Polteageist is threatened, Carracosta's Sturdy guarantees it survives one hit and Shell Smash on a 74/85 body behind Solid Rock is the slower, tougher version of the same plan. Reserves & disruption: Weavile's Knock Off strips the White Herb or Focus Sash the player is relying on and Icicle Crash covers the Flying answers. Counterplay & audit: Fake Out and Taunt beat both setup lines, Haze undoes them, and Dark and Ghost pressure removes the frail bodies. Could this team be cooler? The old block was Bruxish, Weavile, Wailord and Polteageist - a whale inside a mountain tomb, and Wailord and Bruxish are both wanted elsewhere. It is cooler now because it commits to the location: Aqua looting a graveyard means a haunted teapot, a witch's hat and a fossil turtle, and the room's idea is that a bought turn becomes a Shell Smash twice over. Cursed Body on Polteageist also makes the player's strongest attack a gamble - disabling it is a real, visible consequence.

Alternate deployment: Lumineon's Storm Drain is the room's redirection - it pulls every single-target Water attack on the field to itself, gains +1 Special Attack for each, and it is the Water immunity the player does not expect from a fish. Reserves & disruption: Drifblim's Aftermath punishes the contact knockout and Unburden-free bulk holds a slot for the room's duration. Counterplay & audit: Taunt the setter, Fairy pressure on Spiritomb, spread Water moves ignore Storm Drain, and running out the five turns is always available. Could this team be cooler? The old block was Jellicent, Amoonguss, Lanturn and Golisopod - a Grass mushroom redirecting on a mountain of the dead, and three species other rooms now own. Storm Drain instead of Rage Powder also means Safety Goggles - the player's usual answer - does nothing.

primary_question: Can the player beat this grunt team (Glimmora, Swalot, Mightyena, Camerupt) on its own terms: Room one of the raid, the slag door. First two useful turns: Glimmora attacks with Power Gem or Sludge Wave; if the player answers it with a physical hit, Toxic Debris lays Toxic Spikes for free and every later Magma room profits, so Mortal Spin is only for clearing the player's own hazards. Swalot Yawns the target it cannot remove more profitably and Encores a committed setup or protect. Alternate deployment: Camerupt is the faction mount and the room's only real damage spike; Mightyena is the faction dog with Intimidate and a Band. Reserves & disruption: Toxic Spikes are the hideout's shared opening investment; a grounded Poison switch-in absorbs them. Counterplay & audit: fly or levitate past the spikes, Ground and Water pressure, Taunt the Yawn, and Safety Goggles or Misty ground are not answers here. Could this team be cooler? Chip Torkoal and the room's damage collapses - that is the lesson the player needs before Maxie.

primary_question: Can the player beat this admin team (Gigalith, Excadrill, Coalossal, Volcanion, Krookodile, Golurk) on its own terms: Tabitha runs the excavation, so his battle is the hideout's sand engine executed properly. First two useful turns: Gigalith's Sand Stream with Smooth Rock lasts eight turns and Excadrill's Sand Rush doubles its Speed for all of them, so the opening is Gigalith attacking while Excadrill outruns almost anything the player owns. Gigalith's own alternative action is Wide Guard when the player's answer to a Rock-heavy admin is a spread move. Alternate deployment: Coalossal's Steam Engine is NOT self-activated here - the previous Mt Chimney fight already used that trick and repeating it would be a weaker second showing. Instead Coalossal is a trap: any Fire or Water attack the player aims at it, including the Water attack that is 4x super effective and the obvious answer to a Rock/Fire body, grants +6 Speed if it survives, and Weakness Policy grants +2/+2 on top. Killing it outright is correct; chipping it is a disaster. Reserves & disruption: Volcanion is the faction's captured volcano spirit and Steam Eruption off Choice Specs is the admin's raw damage; Krookodile's Moxie converts a knockout into a sweep. Mega Golurk with Iron Fist is the ace and its Shadow Punch and Drain Punch are both boosted. Counterplay & audit: one large hit on Coalossal rather than two, weather replacement to strip Sand Rush, Wide Guard against the paired Rock lane, and Water/Ground pressure. Could this team be cooler? The previous build had Dragapult firing Surf at its own Coalossal - a 4x super effective Water attack on a Rock/Fire ally, which is a genuine design defect, not a clever combo, and Dragapult is a Ghost dragon with no Magma identity. It is cooler now because removing the broken self-hit turns Coalossal into the fight's real puzzle, because Excadrill here foreshadows the Mega Excadrill Tabitha brings to the Space Center, and because Volcanion - literally the volcano Pokemon - is the correct legendary for a man who digs into volcanoes.

primary_question: Can the player beat this admin team (Ninetales, Chi Yu, Great Tusk, Ceruledge, Salazzle, Pyroar) on its own terms: Courtney is the faction's analyst and her battle is the sun engine executed properly. First two useful turns: Ninetales' Drought is automatic; its own action is Encore, which locks a player who took a setup or protect turn into repeating it, or a sun-boosted Heat Wave. Great Tusk's Protosynthesis triggers on that sun and raises its already enormous Attack, so Headlong Rush lands on turn one. Alternate deployment: Chi-Yu's Beads of Ruin cuts every other Pokemon's Special Defense by 25 percent for as long as it is on the field - a permanent, field-wide debuff that makes Ninetales' and Ceruledge's special lanes hit far harder than their stats suggest, and the player will not see it in the battle text. Reserves & disruption: Salazzle's Corrosion poisons Steel and Poison types, which is how Courtney answers the Steel walls the player brings to a Fire team; Ceruledge's Bitter Blade heals it for half the damage dealt and Weak Armor turns the player's physical answer into +2 Speed. Mega Pyroar is the ace and Competitive means any stat drop hands it +2 Special Attack. Counterplay & audit: remove Chi-Yu early even though it is not the immediate threat, replace the sun, and do not use Intimidate or Icy Wind into Competitive. Could this team be cooler? The previous build's sixth was a second Houndoom, which duplicated Flash Fire with the rest of the team and added nothing. It is cooler now with Ceruledge: a Fire/Ghost blade spirit gives Courtney a physical lane, Ghost coverage against the Psychic answers to her, self-healing that makes chip damage pointless, and Weak Armor so that the player's physical response accelerates her rather than her opponent. Chi-Yu's invisible team-wide Special Defense cut remains the fight's best hidden interaction.

primary_question: Can the player beat this leader team (Stakataka, Regirock, Rhyperior, Copperajah, Garganacl, Camerupt) on its own terms: Maxie wants to raise the continent, so the boss fight is the land itself refusing to move at your speed. First two useful turns: Stakataka sets Trick Room - it has zero Speed IVs and 13 base Speed, so it moves last in normal order and first under its own room, and Wide Guard is its alternative when the player's answer to six slow bodies is a spread move. Under the reversed order every other member outruns almost the entire player team. Alternate deployment: Mega Camerupt is the payoff. Quiet, zero Speed, Solid Rock, and Eruption at full HP is 150 base power into both slots from a Mega Special Attack stat - the single largest attack in the campaign to this point - and Trick Room means it fires first rather than last. Reserves & disruption: Regirock uses Curse, which is normally a liability because it lowers Speed; under Trick Room lowering Speed makes it faster, so Curse is pure profit and it becomes an unkillable +2 attacker. Copperajah's Heavy Metal and Rhyperior's Solid Rock are the two bodies that hold the field while the room ticks; Rhyperior's Lightning Rod also draws the Electric attacks aimed at nothing else here. Counterplay & audit: Taunt the setter, Protect or stall the five turns and win the turns after, Fake Out to deny the room turn, Haze the Curses, and chip Mega Camerupt so Eruption weakens. Could this team be cooler? The previous build was Torkoal/Crobat/Mightyena/Victreebel/Hydreigon/Mega Camerupt - which is very nearly the same team Maxie already brought to Mt Chimney, plus a Hydreigon that belongs to no faction. Fighting the same man twice with the same sun-and-Tailwind plan is the weakest thing a villain leader can do. It is cooler now because the second Maxie fight is a completely different machine from the first: Mt Chimney was sun and speed, the hideout is Trick Room and stone, and the same Mega Camerupt that was a slow liability there is the whole point here. Curse under Trick Room, Beast Boost on a fortress, and a full-HP Eruption arriving first are three interactions the player has not seen from this faction before.

First two useful turns: Clawitzer's Mega Launcher doubles every pulse move it owns, and the room's signature is that this includes Heal Pulse - a full half of an ally's maximum HP restored in one action, from a grunt. The crew's plan is therefore to keep Mega Eelektross alive through damage the player expected to be lethal. Crobat Taunts the setup or support the player needs, or pivots with U-turn. Alternate deployment: Mega Eelektross has no weaknesses while Levitate holds and Wild Charge plus Crunch covers the field; it is the ace and the Mega slot. Reserves & disruption: Alolan Muk's Poison/Dark typing is immune to Psychic and its Knock Off strips the item the player was relying on. Counterplay & audit: Taunt or Encore the healer, burst damage that outpaces a 50 percent heal, Ground attacks the moment Levitate is off, and Fairy pressure on the Dark bodies. Could this team be cooler? The old block had the same four members but Clawitzer was a plain three-pulse attacker, which wasted the one ability in the game that turns a support move into a game-changer. It is cooler now because a grunt with a Mega and a doubled Heal Pulse is a genuine difficulty spike that the player will remember and complain about in the right way - and because the counterplay is clean and teachable: Taunt the shrimp, not the eel.

First two useful turns: Toxicroak's Fake Out buys the turn, and Pyukumuku is the reason the room is dangerous - Innards Out means that whoever lands the knockout blow immediately takes damage equal to Pyukumuku's remaining HP, so the player must choose between leaving a Recover-spamming wall alive and killing it into a full-HP retaliation. Wishiwashi opens in Solo Form and flips to School Form above a quarter HP, so it looks like free damage and is not. Alternate deployment: Overqwil's Intimidate plus Swords Dance is the physical lane once the stall bodies have soaked two turns. Reserves & disruption: Toxicroak's Dry Skin heals it on the Water attacks the player brought for this whole hideout. Counterplay & audit: chip Pyukumuku with a Pokemon you are willing to lose, or ignore it; Psychic and Ground pressure on the Poison pair; Electric and Grass on Wishiwashi. Could this team be cooler? The old block repeated Toxapex from the hull-breaker room and finished with Falinks, a Roman phalanx of bugs that has no place on a pirate crew. It is cooler now because it commits fully to being the attrition room - Innards Out, Schooling and Dry Skin are three separate ways of making the player's damage not count - and because Innards Out is the single most memorable "wait, what just happened" interaction available at this stage and no other trainer in the campaign has it.

That gives Hawlucha +1 Defense and triggers Unburden, doubling its Speed for the rest of the battle; a Swords Dance behind that is the pair's win condition. Rillaboom's own opening is Fake Out or a terrain-boosted Grassy Glide, which is priority while the terrain holds. Reserves & disruption: Tsareena's Queenly Majesty blocks every priority move aimed at this side, which is the standard answer to a doubled-Speed sweeper, and Trop Kick lowers the target's Attack on every hit. Counterplay & audit: Flying types, Levitate and Safety Goggles all ignore Rage Powder; replacing the terrain stops the healing and Grassy Glide's priority; Fire, Ice and Flying pressure answers all four. Could this team be cooler? It is cooler now because Grassy Seed Unburden Hawlucha is a famous, spectacular doubles engine that appears nowhere else in the campaign, because the four members form one chain rather than two pairs, and because Queenly Majesty and Rage Powder give the team two different, honest ways of protecting the sweeper.

The concrete judgement: Wish-passing beside an Eviolite Hustle attacker is a real, small engine, it is thematically a nurse and her half-trained dragon, and it gives an ordinary fight one decision the player has to get right, which is whether to spend two attacks on Zweilous or let Wish undo the first one.

The concrete judgement: Compound Eyes Sleep Powder is one of the few things an ordinary trainer owns that can genuinely end a player's battle on turn one, and pairing it with Rage Powder on the same Pokemon forces a real decision - the player must choose between answering the sleep and answering the redirection, and Butterfree is frail enough that killing it solves both. That is a complete, fair encounter at this level and it does not need a rarer species to be interesting.

Reserves & disruption: Mr. Mime and Mr. Rime both carry Ally Switch, so a committed attack can land on the wrong target entirely; Mr. Rime's Screen Cleaner is a deliberate irony the AI must not use on its own screens. Starmie's Analytic makes it the damage that arrives after everything else has moved. The old room had Klefki and Metang bolted onto two screen setters, with no reason for the six to be together. It is cooler now because it is the gym's positioning puzzle rather than its bulk puzzle: priority is switched off by Armor Tail, targeting is unreliable because of two Ally Switch users, and damage is halved by screens. The player has to give up precision and win on raw output.

First two useful turns: Wobbuffet's Shadow Tag prevents every non-Ghost opponent from switching out, and it has no attacking move at all - Counter returns double a physical hit, Mirror Coat returns double a special one, and Encore locks the player into whatever they just did. The correct read against Wobbuffet is to do nothing large, which is exactly what Samantha's partners need. Alternate deployment: with the player pinned, Reuniclus takes Calm Mind behind Magic Guard, which means Life Orb recoil, poison, burn, sandstorm and hazards all deal it zero damage, and Swoobat's Simple doubles every stat change so one Calm Mind is +2/+2. Reserves & disruption: Munkidori's Toxic Chain badly poisons on roughly a third of its hits with no move slot spent, which beats the stall the player would otherwise use to outlast the trap; male Indeedee and Azelf are the immediate special pressure. Counterplay & audit: a Ghost-typed member ignores Shadow Tag entirely, Taunt stops the Calm Minds, and Knock Off or a U-turn-free pivot plan is essential before entering. Could this team be cooler? The old room had Gothitelle and Grimmsnarl doing two unrelated jobs. It is cooler now because it is one idea executed without compromise: you cannot switch, and the thing preventing you cannot be safely attacked. Swoobat's Simple is the piece worth pointing at - a Pokemon nobody rates becomes a +2 sweeper in a single turn behind a wall that punishes both attack categories.

Only Dondozo acts during the occupied turns, so the room is a single enormous body rather than two, and Order Up gains an extra boost from the Curly form inside it. Alternate deployment: female Indeedee's Psychic Surge covers the floor in Psychic Terrain, which blocks every priority move against grounded targets - the answer a player reaches for against a +2 wall - and turns Expanding Force into a spread attack at 120 base power. Terrain Extender holds it eight turns. Reserves & disruption: Indeedee also has Follow Me, so she can redirect a committed attack away from Dondozo entirely, and After You can hand Dondozo the turn order it lacks. Wyrdeer's Intimidate cuts the physical answers and Musharna's Telepathy makes it immune to spread damage from its own partner. Counterplay & audit: knock out Tatsugiri before they pair, or remove Dondozo with special damage while the boosts are only defensive; Grass and Electric pressure; terrain replacement restores your priority. Could this team be cooler? The old room already had the Commander pair and Indeedee, but Sigilyph and Dusknoir were bolted on with no relation to either engine. It is cooler now because every remaining slot serves the same plan: Follow Me protects the whale, Psychic Terrain switches off the priority that answers it, Intimidate blunts the physical answer and Telepathy makes the partner immune to the collateral. It is the most tightly built room in the gym and the hardest to unpick in one turn.

primary_question: Can the player beat this gym team (Metang, Girafarig, Duosion, Kadabra, Elgyem, Victini) on its own terms: Room nine: the apprentices. First two useful turns: five of Macey's six are unevolved Pokemon holding Eviolite, which raises their Defense and Special Defense by 50 percent each - Metang, Girafarig, Duosion, Kadabra and Elgyem are all individually far bulkier than the player expects, and the room's whole plan is to be un-knockable for long enough that Victini's Victory Star makes the accuracy of every attack on Macey's side 1.3x. Metang opens with Earthquake; Elgyem's Telepathy makes it immune to that Earthquake, which is the room's one clean doubles interaction. Alternate deployment: Duosion's Magic Guard plus Eviolite means Life Orb, poison, hazards and weather do nothing to it while it Calm Minds; Girafarig's Sap Sipper turns the Grass attacks the player brought for a Psychic gym into +1 Attack. Reserves & disruption: Kadabra's Magic Guard and Encore lock a player who spent a turn setting up; Victini is the ace and V-create is the largest single attack any non-leader in the gym owns. Counterplay & audit: Knock Off removes Eviolite and the room collapses; spread moves beat the bulk faster than single targets; Dark, Bug and Ghost pressure. Could this team be cooler? The old room was Ferrothorn, Toxapex, Slowking and Reuniclus - a stall pile shared with three other rooms and no identity. It is cooler now because "the gym's student room, where the students have not evolved yet and are still a serious problem" is a concept the player can read off the screen, because five Eviolite bodies is a genuinely awkward thing to break through, and because Knock Off - a move most players carry and rarely think about - is the exact key to the door.

primary_question: Can the player beat this gym team (Pincurchin, Raichu Alola, Rotom Mow, Aegislash, Magearna, Porygon Z) on its own terms: Room ten: Electric Terrain, the gym's machine room. First two useful turns: Pincurchin's Electric Surge is automatic and Terrain Extender holds it eight turns; the terrain boosts Electric moves by 30 percent, prevents every grounded Pokemon from falling asleep, and blocks priority against grounded targets - so the player's Fake Out, Sucker Punch and Extreme Speed answers to a slow room simply fail. Alolan Raichu's Surge Surfer doubles its Speed in that terrain and it is the room's sweeper. Alternate deployment: Magearna's Soul-Heart raises its Special Attack by one stage every time any Pokemon on the field faints, so a long fight makes it progressively unanswerable, and Fleur Cannon off that stack ends rooms. Reserves & disruption: Aegislash switches to Blade Forme when it attacks and back to Shield Forme with King's Shield, which also cuts the Attack of anything that touched it; Rotom-Mow's Levitate keeps it out of the Ground answers and Leaf Storm covers them. Counterplay & audit: replace the terrain and both the speed and the priority block disappear at once, Ground attacks answer four of the six, and Fire and Fighting pressure removes the Steel bodies. Could this team be cooler? The old room shared Grumpig, Beheeyem and Espathra with three other rooms and never explained why an Electric Pokemon was in a Psychic gym. It is cooler now because the terrain is doing three separate jobs the player can feel - damage, sleep immunity and priority denial - and because Magearna's Soul-Heart makes the room actively harder the better the player is doing. Pincurchin is a deliberately unglamorous engine holding up two of the rarest bodies in the gym. Magearna holds Magearnite: the room's Soul-Heart artillery Mega-Evolves when the terrain damage has already forced a knockout, so the stone rewards the room's own plan rather than replacing it.

=== ENCOUNTER 0398 ===
physical_group_id: PHYSICAL_MOSSDEEPCITY_GYM_0297
proposed_encounter_id: PHYSICAL_MOSSDEEPCITY_GYM_0297
campaign_order: 398
atlas_ordinal: 398
chapter: Mind Badge
strict_cap: 60
location: MossdeepCity_Gym
requirement: optional
status: master_audited_ready_for_implementation
battle_class: gym
ai_profile: sharp
primary_question: Can the player beat this gym team (Sableye, Bronzor, Banette, Mr Mime Galar, Dusknoir, Necrozma) on its own terms: Room eleven: Gravity, and the gym's last idea before the twins. First two useful turns: Sableye has Prankster, so its Gravity goes up with priority on turn one; Bronzor is the backup setter, so removing the Focus Sash imp does not end the room. Under Gravity every move on the field gains roughly 67 percent relative accuracy, every Flying type and every Levitate user is dragged to the ground and becomes hittable by Ground attacks, and Fly, Bounce and Magnet Rise stop working. Every attacking move in this room is one that normally misses. Alternate deployment: Bronzor's Hypnosis is 60 percent accurate in an ordinary battle and close to certain under its own Gravity, and Galarian Mr. Mime's Vital Spirit makes it immune to that sleep, so the pair can fire it into a crowded board without a partner casualty. Galarian Mr. Mime then attacks with Blizzard and Focus Blast - two 70 percent moves that Gravity repairs - behind a Nasty Plot. Reserves & disruption: Necrozma is the ace and Photon Geyser uses whichever of its attacking stats is higher while ignoring the target's ability, which is the one attack in the gym that a Magic Guard, Levitate or Flash Fire answer cannot blunt; Prism Armor also cuts every super effective hit against it by a quarter. Banette's Cursed Body can disable the move the player was relying on and Destiny Bond takes its killer with it; Choice Band Dusknoir supplies the physical Ground lane that Gravity has just made universally relevant. Note that Bronzor runs Heatproof rather than Levitate on purpose - Gravity would switch Levitate off anyway, so the room is built out of Pokemon that lose nothing by being grounded, which is the discipline the old build did not have. Counterplay & audit: Taunt Sableye before the priority Gravity and then remove Bronzor before it re-sets; bring Ground coverage of your own, because everything is grounded for both sides; Dark, Ghost, Fire and Steel pressure answers the room. Could this team be cooler? The version this audit first wrote was cooler than the old Claydol/Malamar/Gothitelle pile it replaced, but it leaned on Jirachi, Necrozma and Latios - three legendaries in a single gym room, which is not "occasional" and which meant the room won on raw stats rather than on its idea. It is cooler now for the same reason it is more honest: with the legendary crutch removed, every remaining slot has to earn itself through Gravity, and two of them are Pokemon nobody respects. An unevolved Eviolite bell setting the field effect and then landing a guaranteed Hypnosis, beside a Galarian mime who is immune to it and throws a never-missing Blizzard, is a far better memory than a Latios firing an accurate Draco Meteor. Necrozma stays because Photon Geyser under Gravity is the room's thesis - the attack that cannot miss and cannot be turned off by an ability - and one legendary ace is exactly the budget a twelfth-of-a-gym room deserves.

Necrozma stays because Photon Geyser under Gravity is the room's thesis - the attack that cannot miss and cannot be turned off by an ability - and one legendary ace is exactly the budget a twelfth-of-a-gym room deserves.
weakest_link: Taunt Sableye first and be ready for Bronzor to re-set Gravity; Gravity grounds Nicholas' own team too, so Ground coverage is live for both sides; Dark and Ghost pressure on Sableye, Banette and Dusknoir; Fire, Fighting and Ground on Bronzor; Galarian Mr. Mime is frail and dies to any priority; Necrozma folds to Dark and Bug damage once Prism Armor is worn down.

First two useful turns: Solrock and Lunatone enter together - the sun and the moon, the gym's emblem - and Solrock sets Trick Room with a Mental Herb so Taunt cannot stop the first attempt, while Lunatone spends a Power Herb on an instant Meteor Beam, which is a 120 base power Rock attack plus a free +1 Special Attack with no charging turn. That is the twins' opening statement: the room reverses and the first attack is already at full power. Alternate deployment: Tapu Lele's Psychic Surge is the second half of the engine. Psychic Terrain blocks all priority against grounded targets, which is the only fast answer to a Trick Room team, and it boosts Expanding Force into a 120 base power spread move for Hatterene and Gardevoir. Hatterene, at 29 base Speed with Magic Bounce, is both the fastest thing on the field under Trick Room and immune to every status move aimed at it. Reserves & disruption: Cresselia is the twins' durability - Lunar Blessing-free Moonlight, Helping Hand and a second Trick Room so the room can be re-set when it lapses. Mega Gardevoir with Pixilate turns Hyper Voice into a Fairy-typed spread attack off an enormous Special Attack stat, under terrain, under Trick Room, moving first. Counterplay & audit: this is the hardest board in the region to unpick with one action - Taunt is answered by Mental Herb and Magic Bounce, priority is answered by Psychic Terrain, and speed is answered by Trick Room. The honest answers are Wide Guard against the spread attacks, Steel and Poison typing against the Fairy lane, Dark types that ignore the Psychic half entirely, and surviving the five turns. Could this team be cooler? The six species were already right - Solrock and Lunatone are the twins' identity and Tapu Lele, Hatterene, Cresselia and Mega Gardevoir are the correct escalation. What was missing was the statement that the two field effects are one machine: Trick Room decides the order and Psychic Terrain removes the only tool that beats it. primary_question: Can the player beat this ace team (Bronzong, Gourgeist, Heracross, Florges Red, Copperajah, Crabominable) on its own terms: Concept: a genuine Trick Room crew in which every member is deliberately, correctly slow. First two useful turns: Bronzong sets Trick Room when the reversed order actually helps - Mental Herb protects that turn from Taunt - while Gourgeist attacks or burns the biggest physical threat. Turn two spends the room on damage, not on a second support action. Alternate deployment: Bronzong plus Mega Crabominable is the heavy mode, with Iron Fist Ice Hammer and Drain Punch hitting under the reversed order. Reserves & disruption: Guts Heracross converts its Toxic Orb into Facade and Close Combat, Copperajah's Heavy Metal doubles its weight for Heavy Slam, and Florges is a separate Calm Mind/Wish endgame with Flower Veil protecting the team from stat drops. Body Press still reads the user's real Defence. Could this team be cooler? It already had a good idea and a bad implementation: every slow member carried a 31 Speed IV, so the room was fighting its own team. Zeroing Speed IVs on all five Brave/Relaxed/Quiet members is the difference between a Trick Room team and a team with a Trick Room move, and it is the single most valuable change here. Swapping the duplicated Mudsdale for Copperajah keeps the same slow-anvil role while giving the trainer a rarer, heavier signature that actually rewards Heavy Slam, and Mega Crabominable stays as the payoff nobody else in the campaign fields. Overrepresented? Copperajah, Crabominable and Gourgeist are unique; Bronzong and Gothitelle-style room setters are spaced far apart (Conor E0442, Warren E0439 use different setters). theme_and_tempo: Concept: a genuine Trick Room crew in which every member is deliberately, correctly slow. First two useful turns: Bronzong sets Trick Room when the reversed order actually helps - Mental Herb protects that turn from Taunt - while Gourgeist attacks or burns the biggest physical threat. Turn two spends the room on damage, not on a second support action.
