Body Press still reads the user's real Defence. Could this team be cooler? It already had a good idea and a bad implementation: every slow member carried a 31 Speed IV, so the room was fighting its own team. Zeroing Speed IVs on all five Brave/Relaxed/Quiet members is the difference between a Trick Room team and a team with a Trick Room move, and it is the single most valuable change here. Swapping the duplicated Mudsdale for Copperajah keeps the same slow-anvil role while giving the trainer a rarer, heavier signature that actually rewards Heavy Slam, and Mega Crabominable stays as the payoff nobody else in the campaign fields. Overrepresented? Copperajah, Crabominable and Gourgeist are unique; Bronzong and Gothitelle-style room setters are spaced far apart (Conor E0442, Warren E0439 use different setters). Levels: cap 76, offsets 1/1/1/1/1/2.

Turn two uses the actual speed order rather than spending a second support turn. Alternate deployment: Probopass's Wide Guard and Magnet Pull trap-and-shield mode supports Sceptile's White Herb Unburden line, which doubles Sceptile's Speed the moment Leaf Storm's drop is cancelled. Reserves & disruption: Volcarona is the Quiver Dance alternative with Heavy-Duty Boots; Corviknight's Mirror Armor reflects stat drops back at the attacker, including Intimidate. Mega Pidgeot's No Guard cuts both ways - opposing Focus Blast and Hypnosis also cannot miss it. Could this team be cooler? It is much cooler now. First two useful turns: Kingdra sets Rain Dance only when its own Swift Swim or Gyarados's pressure repays the turn, otherwise it opens with Hydro Pump or Draco Meteor; Gyarados attacks after Intimidate or dances when the board is safe. Turn two uses the real weather and speed order. Alternate deployment: Raichu's Fake Out and Lightning Rod hold the field for Kingdra before a deliberately timed Mega, and Lightning Rod draws the Electric attack the Water core fears. Reserves & disruption: Magikarp is a genuine novelty slot - under rain its Swift Swim doubles its Speed and Flail from a Focus Sash-preserved 1 HP is a real, ridiculous knockout; it is not a sixth competitive set and must not be scored as one. Tentacruel covers Poison and speed control. Mega Raichu's ability replaces Lightning Rod, so the redirection stops the moment it transforms. Could this team be cooler? It is already one of the campaign's most characterful ideas and the answer is to protect it rather than replace it: the memorable interaction here is rain plus Focus Sash plus Flail, and a player who ignores Magikarp genuinely loses a Pokemon to it. Adding a legend or a second Mega would kill the joke. The only thing worth tightening is the level spread so the surrounding five are actually threatening enough that the player cannot afford to spend two turns laughing. Overrepresented? Kingdra is also Linda's (E0438) and Juan's ace, but this is the only Rain Dance/Life Orb version; Gyarados's other owners are an Aqua grunt and Juan's Mega; Mega Raichu Y appears only here, with Vito holding Raichu X. Levels: cap 76, offsets 1/1/0/1/2.
weakest_link: Replace the weather and both the sweeper and the joke die. Grass and Electric attacks cover the whole roster, spread damage breaks Magikarp's Sash before it can Flail, and Gyarados is one Rock Slide or Thunderbolt from gone. Deny Fake Out with your own and Raichu has no safe turn.

primary_question: Can the player beat this ace team (Torkoal, Lilligant, Porygon Z, Charizard) on its own terms: Concept: the advanced student's answer to Flannery - the same After You plus Eruption idea, but with a second sun setter so the player cannot simply erase the weather once. First two useful turns: the authored tactic makes Lilligant offer After You to Torkoal when that actually lands a full-power Eruption before the opposing threats move; otherwise Lilligant uses Sleep Powder or Leaf Storm and Torkoal attacks in its own slow order. Turn two rechecks Torkoal's current HP, because Eruption scales with it, and whether the ally has already acted - After You is worthless then. Alternate deployment: Lilligant's sleep and support enable Porygon-Z's Adaptability Tri Attack or a Nasty Plot turn when the sun has been taken away. Reserves & disruption: Mega Charizard Y is the second real Drought, so Lilligant's manual Sunny Day is an emergency reclaim, not mandatory redundancy; Chlorophyll only doubles Lilligant's Speed while sun is actually up. Could this team be cooler? The idea was already strong but it was not executable - the block described an After You engine that no tactic line told the AI to perform, so in play it was a generic sun team. Adding the explicit AFTER_YOU tactic is what turns the concept into the fight the prose promises, and the weather-reclaim second setter is exactly the escalation a post-Flannery sun trainer should have. Beyond that it does not need rarer species; Porygon-Z is the one member a player never prepares for, and that is the fight's real teeth. Overrepresented? Torkoal and Lilligant recur with Flannery and Julie (E0490), which is deliberate - this trainer is explicitly a variation on that theme - but the two sun sources, the Focus Sash Lilligant and the Adaptability pivot make the board play differently. First two useful turns: Abomasnow's Snow Warning is active on entry, so Beartic is already fast; Abomasnow attacks with Wood Hammer or Ice Shard while Medicham opens with Fake Out or a Pure Power Close Combat. Turn two uses the real speed order under snow rather than spending a turn establishing weather that already exists. Alternate deployment: Medicham and Flareon are the weather-independent physical mode - Pure Power and Guts Facade both hit hard with no setup at all. Reserves & disruption: snow raises the Defence of Ice types, so Abomasnow and Beartic are tougher than their listed stats suggest; Flareon's Toxic Orb Guts mode gains nothing from the weather and Charti Berry cushions exactly one Rock attack on Beartic. Could this team be cooler? Yes, and the fix was structural rather than cosmetic. The authored version flagged SNOW while relying on Beartic spending a turn on Snowscape, so the team's own Slush Rush sweeper had to waste the turn it needed to sweep, and the redirecting Amoonguss duplicated Sebastian's team two encounters earlier. Abomasnow solves both at once: automatic snow, a second Ice attacker, a Grass answer to the Water and Ground types that wall the rest, and Ice Shard priority that pairs with Medicham's Fake Out to steal turns. The memorable interaction is now the double opening - Fake Out plus Ice Shard removing a Focus Sash lead before it acts. Overrepresented? Abomasnow's other owner Dianne (E0492) uses a Quiet special Blizzard set in Victory Road, so the physical version here is clearly distinct; Beartic, Medicham and Flareon are unique in the stretch, and Amoonguss now belongs solely to Sebastian (E0412). primary_question: Can the player beat this regular team (Kingdra, Lumineon, Araquanid, Arctozolt) on its own terms: Concept: a squall on the open water - Mega Kingdra calls the rain and three very different bodies exploit it. First two useful turns: Kingdra sets Rain Dance or opens with Muddy Water, which is spread and therefore cannot be stolen by an ally, while Lumineon attacks or sets Tailwind. Turn two stacks Swift Swim on top of Tailwind for a speed tier nothing at this stage matches. Alternate deployment: Araquanid's Wide Guard and Water Bubble mode covers Arctozolt, whose Bolt Beak doubles in power whenever it moves before its target - which is precisely what the rain and Tailwind are for. Reserves & disruption: Sticky Web is a long-term investment and must beat an immediate attack to be worth the turn; Water Bubble doubles Araquanid's Water damage and halves incoming Fire. Could this team be cooler? It is cooler now for one concrete reason. Lumineon previously ran Storm Drain, which meant the team's own single-target Water attacks were being pulled away from their targets by their own partner - a real strategic defect, not a stylistic one. Switching it to Swift Swim removes the self-sabotage and makes Lumineon the second rain abuser the RAIN tag always implied, so the fight now reads as one coherent squall instead of three unrelated Water mons. The Bolt Beak plus double speed control interaction is the thing a player will remember, and it is worth the Mega slot. Overrepresented? Mega Kingdra exists only here; Lumineon's other owner Connie runs the Storm Drain version deliberately, in the one gym room built to use it. Araquanid and Arctozolt are unique in the stretch. Turn two spends the reversed order rather than re-casting the room. Alternate deployment: Cofagrigus is the backup setter for the second half, holding the room open for Mega Drampa's Hyper Voice and Draco Meteor. Reserves & disruption: Torterra and Aggron are the slow physical coverage; Mummy replaces the ability of anything that makes contact with Cofagrigus, which can silently turn off a player's Intimidate, Guts or Multiscale. Telepathy protects Musharna from a partner's spread move, not from opponents. Could this team be cooler? The two-setter structure and the Galvanize trick were good; what made the team weaker than it looked was that every slow member carried a 31 Speed IV, so the room it worked to set was partly wasted on its own side. Zeroing Speed on all five Brave/Quiet/Sassy members is the change that makes the concept function, and Cofagrigus's Mummy is now worth calling out as the signature interaction - a player whose Intimidate lead punches it loses the ability for the rest of the fight. The species set is already unusual enough for a route ace and does not need replacing. Overrepresented? Alolan Golem, Drampa, Cofagrigus and Musharna are unique in the campaign; Torterra recurs only with Owen (E0488) in Victory Road, and the neighbouring room teams (Herman E0422, Conor E0442) use entirely different setters and payoffs. primary_question: Can the player beat this ace team (Gengar, Carracosta, Aromatisse, Rotom Frost) on its own terms: Concept: a haunted-cold quartet with no weather and no setup - four immediate threats and one very deliberate accuracy gamble. First two useful turns: Gengar attacks or uses Icy Wind for speed control while Carracosta attacks or selects Wide Guard against a genuine spread threat. Turn two acts on the resulting order instead of assuming every attack is now safe. Alternate deployment: Aromatisse's Helping Hand and Wish support Rotom-Frost's Blizzard and Thunderbolt coverage; Aroma Veil protects the pair from Taunt, Encore and Attract but not from damage or ordinary status. Reserves & disruption: Rotom-Frost's Blizzard is its form's signature attack and there is no snow in this team, so it is a knowingly inaccurate 110-power gamble - the Wide Lens is the honest fix rather than pretending a weather source exists. Rock Gem is a single-use Rock Slide amplifier on Carracosta and Sturdy guarantees it survives one hit to use it. Could this team be cooler? The unusual part - a Ghost, a fossil turtle, a perfumer and an appliance ghost with no shared engine - is actually the point: this is a fight about four independent threats rather than one combo, which is a welcome change of pace between two Trick Room aces. The change it needed was honesty about Blizzard. Wide Lens is a small, legal, in-character fix that makes the gamble a real 91% threat rather than a coin flip, and it keeps Rotom-Frost's identity intact instead of replacing a rare form with a safer one. Overrepresented? Rotom-Frost, Carracosta's Rock Gem set and Aromatisse are unique; Gengar's other campaign owners are Samuel - retooled to Mismagius in this pass - Leaf's Kanto team and Phoebe's Mega, so this remains the only Focus Sash Icy Wind version. The unusual part - a Ghost, a fossil turtle, a perfumer and an appliance ghost with no shared engine - is actually the point: this is a fight about four independent threats rather than one combo, which is a welcome change of pace between two Trick Room aces. The change it needed was honesty about Blizzard. Wide Lens is a small, legal, in-character fix that makes the gamble a real 91% threat rather than a coin flip, and it keeps Rotom-Frost's identity intact instead of replacing a rare form with a safer one. Overrepresented? Rotom-Frost, Carracosta's Rock Gem set and Aromatisse are unique; Gengar's other campaign owners are Samuel - retooled to Mismagius in this pass - Leaf's Kanto team and Phoebe's Mega, so this remains the only Focus Sash Icy Wind version. Levels: cap 76, offsets 1/1/1/2.
intentional_weakness: Dark, Ground and Rock attacks hit three of the four, and Aromatisse's Aroma Veil does not stop damage. Single-target attacks walk around Wide Guard; Wish only pays out at the end of the following turn, so kill the recipient first. Blizzard can still miss.

primary_question: Can the player beat this ace team (Hariyama, Gothitelle, Ferrothorn, Avalugg) on its own terms: Concept: a trapper's room - Shadow Tag means the player cannot simply switch out of the reversed speed order. First two useful turns: Hariyama's Fake Out buys Gothitelle the turn it needs to set Trick Room; turn two attacks into the reversed order or uses Helping Hand at a concrete knockout threshold. Alternate deployment: Gothitelle and Ferrothorn are the grinding mode - Leech Seed, Iron Barbs and Gyro Ball punish contact and passivity while the trap holds. Reserves & disruption: Avalugg brings Wide Guard, Body Press and Recover but has no Trick Room of its own, so it must be deployed while the room is still running. Shadow Tag stops switching, not targeting, and does not protect the setter from being attacked; Ghost types and Shed Shell ignore it entirely. The Wiki Berry restores HP at low health and is Modest-safe because Gothitelle's Quiet nature does not lower Special Attack. Could this team be cooler? The trap-plus-room pairing is genuinely nasty and is the right identity for this slot, but like the other room teams here it was quietly sabotaging itself with 31 Speed IVs on every slow member. Fixing that is the change that makes the concept real. primary_question: Can the player beat this regular team (Poliwrath, Raticate, Golduck, Lanturn) on its own terms: Concept: a sailor who beats weather teams by refusing to have any - three different absorption abilities and a Cloud Nine switch that turns everyone else's engine off. First two useful turns: Poliwrath attacks while Raticate either attacks or takes its Flame Orb turn; turn two often U-turns into whichever immunity the opposing board has just revealed it needs. Alternate deployment: Cloud Nine Golduck and Volt Absorb Lanturn are the weather-suppression mode - while Golduck is on the field neither side gets rain, sun, sand or snow benefits, which is a real answer to the rain teams that dominate this stretch of coast. Reserves & disruption: Water Absorb, Volt Absorb and Cloud Nine solve three different problems and none of them is general damage reduction; Cloud Nine suppresses weather effects while active but does not clear the weather, so it returns the moment Golduck leaves. Could this team be cooler? It is the right kind of cool already, and the honest judgement is that its value is positional rather than flashy: dropped between Linda's squall, Ronald's rain and the Seafloor Cavern, a deliberate anti-weather sailor is a better encounter than another Swift Swim team would be, and the three-immunity structure teaches the player to check abilities before choosing a spread attack. The improvement it wanted was threat, not novelty - Raticate's Guts Facade and the U-turn pivot are what punish a lazy switch, so the levels rise and the pivot pair leads. Overrepresented? Golduck's Cloud Nine role recurs once, with Annika's Sootopolis room, where it is used to suppress that gym's own rain - a deliberate echo. Poliwrath appears with Santiago and Tiffany in different ability roles; Lanturn's other owner is Crissy's gym room; Raticate is unique. Levels: cap 76, offsets 0/1/1/1.

Turn two attacks through the control or repositions after powder denial. Alternate deployment: Talonflame's Gale Wings gives Brave Bird priority while it is at full HP, which supports Mega Chesnaught's slow physical pressure and provides Tailwind if the board turns into a speed race. Reserves & disruption: this Venusaur has Overgrow, not Chlorophyll or Thick Fat, and there is no sun - do not assume a remembered species ability. Bulletproof makes Chesnaught immune to ball and bomb moves including Sludge Bomb, Shadow Ball and Focus Blast, and Spiky Shield damages contact attackers that try to break a protect. Could this team be cooler? The Bug Gem and Bulletproof ideas were already good; the weak link was a third Arcanine-shaped Intimidate body doing the same job as Susie's two encounters earlier. Talonflame is both rarer and more interesting: Gale Wings priority Brave Bird changes how the player must sequence a knockout, and the Gale Wings-at-full-HP condition gives the player a lever - chip it once and the priority is gone. That is a genuine interaction rather than a stat swap. Overrepresented? primary_question: Can the player beat this admin team (Qwilfish Hisui, Politoed, Keldeo, Ludicolo, Crawdaunt, Dragalge) on its own terms: Concept: Archie's lieutenant and the cavern's first real wall - she brings the rain the boss will inherit, and every member of her crew is built to use it. First two useful turns: Politoed's Drizzle is live on entry and Damp Rock stretches it to eight turns; it supports Choice Specs Keldeo with Helping Hand or slows the board with Icy Wind while Keldeo fires. Turn two respects Keldeo's lock and the actual weather state rather than assuming both. Alternate deployment: Swift Swim Ludicolo is the rain sweeper and answers the Grass and Water types that wall the rest; Hisuian Qwilfish fronts with Intimidate and Eviolite bulk while Barb Barrage doubles in power against an already-poisoned target. Reserves & disruption: Crawdaunt is the Adaptability priority reserve whose Aqua Jet ignores the speed war entirely, and Mega Dragalge is the special Dragon/Poison lane with Adaptability behind it. Secret Sword deals physical damage using Keldeo's Special Attack, which is why the Specs set works; Justified does not make it a physical attacker. Could this team be cooler? Yes - and the version that reaches the player now is. Clefable's Follow Me was a competent but entirely non-Aqua slot: a Fairy support in a pirate hideout, doing a job the faction has no business doing. Hisuian Qwilfish replaces it with something that reads as Shelly's own prized fish, keeps an Intimidate body in the lead slot, and sets up its own Barb Barrage payoff through Muk's and Dragalge's poison. The result is six water/dark/poison bodies, one weather, and three separate ways to convert it - which is what an admin fight should be before the boss does the same thing bigger. Overrepresented? Politoed's Drizzle recurs with Juan four encounters later, which is intentional contrast - Shelly uses rain for burst, Juan uses it for attrition - and Archie now runs Pelipper instead, so the three rain bosses use three different setters. Keldeo, Crawdaunt and Mega Dragalge are unique in the campaign. Levels: cap 84, offsets 2/3/3/2/3/3 - a clear step above the grunt rooms and below Archie.

Turn two spends the speed or the boost instead of adding a second setup on the same side. Alternate deployment: Toxapex's Regenerator, Baneful Bunker and Haze mode is the attrition lead - Baneful Bunker protects and poisons whatever makes contact, and Haze erases the player's boosts as well as its own team's. Toxapex recurs with Juan's gym in a Wide Guard support role rather than this Haze/Bunker one; Mandibuzz, Skuntank and this Lum Berry Gyarados are otherwise unique, and Arbok is returned to Maxie alone. primary_question: Can the player beat this grunt team (Wailord, Seaking, Drapion, Morpeko) on its own terms: Concept: the whale room - the cavern's artillery piece. Wailord brings its own storm and fires a Water Spout that is only terrifying while it is still healthy. First two useful turns: Wailord establishes rain on entry and chooses Water Spout from its execution-time HP, which is why the player must damage it before it acts rather than after; Seaking attacks under Swift Swim, already doubled by its partner's weather. Turn two switches to Hydro Pump once Wailord's HP has fallen far enough that Spout is the weaker option. Alternate deployment: Drapion and Morpeko are the independent physical and control mode that does not care about weather - Sniper turns Drapion's Scope Lens critical hits into genuine removals, and Parting Shot drops both of a target's attacking stats before pivoting. Reserves & disruption: Hunger Switch flips Morpeko's form and therefore Aura Wheel's type at the end of every turn, so the same move is Electric on one turn and Dark on the next; plan around the current form, not the remembered one. Could this team be cooler? The Water Spout artillery idea is one of the best in the Aqua arc and stays. Its defect was self-inflicted: Seaking carried Lightning Rod, which meant the team's own Morpeko had its Electric Aura Wheel pulled away by its partner half the time - a real bug in the plan, not a nuance. Swift Swim fixes it and simultaneously makes Seaking a second rain abuser, so the room finally plays as one rainstorm with a cannon in it. The alternating Aura Wheel type is now a genuine read-the-board puzzle rather than an accident. Overrepresented? Wailord's Drizzle set, Drapion and Morpeko are unique in the campaign; Seaking's other owner Connie deliberately keeps Lightning Rod because her entire gym room is built on redirection. Levels: cap 84, offsets 2/2/2/2.

Turn two attacks under the doubled Speed or pivots when the weather has been denied. Alternate deployment: Overqwil's Intimidate fronts for Bruxish, whose Strong Jaw makes Psychic Fangs, Crunch and Bite genuinely oversized - and Psychic Fangs additionally removes Reflect and Light Screen, so a player hiding behind screens loses them on the same turn they take the hit. Reserves & disruption: Wave Crash costs Bruxish a third of the damage dealt as recoil; Defiant means any stat drop aimed at Purugly - including an opposing Intimidate - raises its Attack by two stages instead. Could this team be cooler? Yes, and it needed to be. The authored room ended with Toxapex and Overqwil both playing defence, so once Gorebyss fell the last door of an Aqua raid turned into a stall match - exactly the wrong note before the boss. Bruxish replaces the wall with a rare, vicious Water/Psychic biter that keeps the pressure up, breaks screens, and gives the room a real identity: the jaws room, where Fake Out, Intimidate and Defiant all interact on the first turn. Overqwil's Intimidate now has an aggressive partner to protect rather than a second wall to hide behind. Overrepresented? Bruxish and Gorebyss are unique in the campaign; Toxapex is moved to the brig room (E0455) where its Haze has a purpose; Purugly and Overqwil appear once each elsewhere in different roles. Could this team be cooler? Yes, and it needed to be. The authored room ended with Toxapex and Overqwil both playing defence, so once Gorebyss fell the last door of an Aqua raid turned into a stall match - exactly the wrong note before the boss. Bruxish replaces the wall with a rare, vicious Water/Psychic biter that keeps the pressure up, breaks screens, and gives the room a real identity: the jaws room, where Fake Out, Intimidate and Defiant all interact on the first turn. Overqwil's Intimidate now has an aggressive partner to protect rather than a second wall to hide behind. Overrepresented? Bruxish and Gorebyss are unique in the campaign; Toxapex is moved to the brig room (E0455) where its Haze has a purpose; Purugly and Overqwil appear once each elsewhere in different roles. Levels: cap 84, offsets 2/2/2/2.
intentional_weakness: Do not use Intimidate into Defiant. Grass and Electric attacks cover the Water half, Dark and Bug hit Bruxish, and Ground answers Overqwil. Replace the weather and Gorebyss is slow and frail; deny Fake Out with your own and the rain turn never happens.

battle_class: leader
ai_profile: master
primary_question: Can the player beat this leader team (Pelipper, Toxicroak, Seismitoad, Dhelmise, Muk Alola, Sharpedo) on its own terms: Concept: the Aqua apex. Archie does not borrow the sea's power yet - he commands a storm of his own and six bodies that each convert it differently, and every one of them is a pirate before it is a Water type. First two useful turns: Pelipper's Drizzle is live the moment the fight starts and Damp Rock holds it for eight turns; it opens with Wide Guard against a spread lead, Tailwind when the board is a speed race, or Hurricane, which never misses in its own rain. Toxicroak leads beside it with Fake Out, stealing the player's first action while Dry Skin heals it every turn the storm lasts - a Water-immune, self-healing Fake Out lead is the single hardest opening in the Aqua arc. Turn two commits to the real board: Seismitoad's Swift Swim is already doubled, so Hydro Pump and Earth Power come before most of the player's team can answer. Alternate deployment: Dhelmise is the ghost ship's anchor and the fight's signature - Anchor Shot deals Steelworker-boosted damage and traps the target, so a player who was planning to switch out of Archie's rain simply cannot, and Power Whip covers the Grass and Water types that expect to wall this roster. Alolan Muk is the weather-independent lane: Poison/Dark typing, Knock Off, Gunk Shot, and Poison Touch on contact, so the fight does not end when the rain does. Reserves & disruption: Mega Sharpedo is the closer, and its base Speed Boost must be earned before transforming, because the Mega ability replaces it - Archie's Mega is a deliberate foreshadow of the Elite Four's Dark specialist, not a coincidence. Toxicroak's Dry Skin is a liability in sun and Fire, Seismitoad's Speed halves when the weather is replaced, and Dhelmise's trap is broken by Ghost types and Shed Shell. Preserve the chronology repair: Kyogre is not awakened yet and must never appear on this team; Archie's power at this point comes from preparation, not the legend, and the roster is built to beat Maxie's Mt. Chimney and Mossdeep fights on its own merits. Could this team be cooler? Emphatically, and it now is. The authored roster was the weakest boss in the villain arc - Goodra, Eelektross, Tentacruel and Poliwrath were generic bulk with no shared engine, two of them duplicated route trainers the player had just beaten, and nothing on the team punished a player for the switching and stalling that beats rain. The rebuild gives Archie four things he did not have: a Fake Out lead that heals in his own weather, a Swift Swim sweeper that uses the storm on turn one, a trapping move that forbids the standard counterplay, and a non-Water fallback in Alolan Muk so removing the rain does not remove the fight. Every member is now water, dark, poison or drowned-ship in flavour, which is exactly the piratical identity the faction was supposed to have, and the fight ends on a Mega rather than opening on one. Overrepresented? Pelipper's other owner is Bridget's fossil-rain gym room, a different weather payoff entirely; Toxicroak, Dhelmise and Alolan Muk appear nowhere else in the campaign; Seismitoad's other owner Tiffany runs the Water Absorb version in the Sootopolis gym. Levels: cap 84, offsets 3/3/4/3/3/5 - the highest pre-badge-eight opponent in the game and a clear step above both Maxie fights.

ai_profile: sharp
primary_question: Can the player beat this gym team (Cloyster, Floatzel, Jellicent, Qwilfish, Simipour, Basculin) on its own terms: Concept: room one of eleven - the volley room. Sootopolis opens by teaching the player that a Water gym can simply out-damage them, with Skill Link multi-hit attacks that ignore Substitutes, Focus Sashes and Sturdy. First two useful turns: Cloyster uses Shell Smash only when Floatzel's Choice Band damage buys it a survivable turn; otherwise both simply attack, because Skill Link Icicle Spear at five hits is already close to a boosted attack. Turn two handles Wave Crash recoil, the Sash and opposing priority before committing the boosted Cloyster. Alternate deployment: Qwilfish's Intimidate and Rocky Helmet front for Simipour's special coverage, which covers the Grass types the rest of the room fears with Grass Knot. Reserves & disruption: Jellicent's Water Absorb, Will-O-Wisp and Recover is the attrition lane and the room's only recovery; Adaptability Basculin is raw immediate pressure with Head Smash as a deliberate all-in. Spikes must beat an immediate attack to be worth its turn against a player with five replacements. Could this team be cooler? The six are a genuinely good spread of Water archetypes and the multi-hit lesson is the right opening note for the gym, so the composition earns retention. What it lacked was weight: as the first of eleven rooms it was authored at flat offsets, which made the gym start soft and never recover. The concrete improvement is a uniform two-level rise with the Adaptability closer higher still, so the player learns in room one that every Sootopolis trainer is a benchmark. Simipour is the one member worth defending explicitly - a Torrent monkey looks like filler, but it is the only member here that answers an opposing Grass lead, and removing it would make the room one-dimensional. Overrepresented? Cloyster, Floatzel, Simipour and Basculin appear only here; Jellicent and Qwilfish each have one distant other owner in different roles, and no other Sootopolis room runs Shell Smash as its headline - Olivia's Carracosta uses a Weakness Policy version with the opposite risk profile. primary_question: Can the player beat this gym team (Lanturn, Swanna, Alomomola, Wishiwashi, Golisopod, Primarina) on its own terms: Concept: room two - the squall room, where the rain is made by hand and three different bodies are built to live inside it. First two useful turns: Swanna sets Rain Dance when its own Weather Ball - which becomes a 100-power Water attack in rain - and Lanturn's pressure both profit; Hydration then cures Swanna's status at the end of every rainy turn, so status is not an answer to it. Lanturn attacks or Volt Switches into the right body. Turn two exploits the actual weather rather than assuming every Water member needs it. Alternate deployment: Alomomola's Regenerator bulk and Mantine-free support line covers Choice Specs Primarina, whose Liquid Voice turns Hyper Voice into a spread Water attack that hits both opposing slots - the room's biggest single click. Reserves & disruption: Wishiwashi is only dangerous in School Form, which requires it to be above one quarter HP at level 20 or higher, so damaging it below that threshold reverts it to a nearly harmless fish mid-fight; Golisopod's Emergency Exit force-switches it at half HP, which interacts badly with its own Choice Band lock and is a real, visible weakness. Could this team be cooler? That is worth keeping. Overrepresented? Alomomola, Swanna, Wishiwashi, Golisopod and Primarina are each unique in the campaign; Lanturn's other owner is the route sailor Hudson in a Volt Absorb role. Bridget's room uses automatic Drizzle instead, so the gym has one manual-rain room and one automatic one by design. Levels: cap 84, offsets 2/2/2/2/2/3.

strict_cap: 70

status: master_audited_ready_for_implementation
battle_class: gym
ai_profile: sharp
primary_question: Can the player beat this gym team (Slowking, Relicanth, Cursola, Quagsire, Overqwil, Avalugg) on its own terms: Concept: room three - the deep, where the water stops moving. This is the gym's Trick Room room: six deliberately slow bodies, zero Speed IVs across the board, and a drowned-coral ghost whose mere presence puts a three-turn clock on anything that touches it. First two useful turns: Slowking sets Trick Room behind a Mental Herb that protects the turn from Taunt, while Relicanth attacks - Rock Head means Head Smash costs it nothing at all, which under reversed order is the hardest single hit in the gym. Turn two spends the room on damage instead of a second support action. Alternate deployment: Quagsire's Unaware ignores every stat boost the player has accumulated, so a Shell Smash or Dragon Dance sweeper walks straight into a wall that does not care; Yawn forces the player to switch or sleep. Reserves & disruption: Cursola's Perish Body starts a three-turn countdown on any attacker that makes contact with it - and on Cursola itself - which turns the room's slowest, frailest member into a genuine threat the player must avoid punching; Strength Sap drains the target's Attack and heals Cursola by that amount. Overqwil's Intimidate and Barb Barrage punish an already-poisoned target, and Avalugg's Body Press and Wide Guard close the room. Could this team be cooler? The authored version was the gym's clear weak point and it is fully redesigned. It was six unconnected Water mons whose own block admitted "the defensive opening must not be the only admissible lead" - a stall room with a Fur Coat Dewgong, an Unaware Quagsire, and then three fast attackers that contradicted them. The rebuild gives the gym the distinct room it was missing and the brief asked for: a real Trick Room room, where Slowking's Regenerator keeps the setter alive across switches, Relicanth's recoil-free Head Smash is the payoff, and Cursola's Perish Body is a memorable interaction found nowhere else in the campaign - the player has to consciously stop making contact. Overrepresented? Cursola, Slowking and Quagsire appear only here; Relicanth is moved out of Olivia's room to give this one its physical payoff, and Avalugg's other owner Conor is a route ace many encounters earlier. The gym's three other slow-ish rooms use Shell Smash, redirection and burst instead, so no engine repeats. Levels: cap 84, offsets 2/2/2/2/2/3.

primary_question: Can the player beat this gym team (Gastrodon, Lumineon, Seaking, Octillery, Huntail, Starmie) on its own terms: Concept: room four - the redirection room, and the gym's cleverest single lesson. Two Storm Drain bodies stand side by side, so Lumineon's Surf damages both opposing slots and simultaneously raises its own partner's Special Attack by one stage. First two useful turns: the authored tactic fires Lumineon's Surf into the board, hitting both opponents while Gastrodon absorbs the friendly half and grows; Gastrodon then attacks with a boosted Earth Power or recovers according to the resulting state. Turn two picks the best real target rather than repeating the mutual boost forever. Alternate deployment: Seaking's Choice Band physical line and Octillery's Sniper special coverage are the mode to use when Storm Drain would get in the team's own way. Reserves & disruption: this is the one room in the gym where allied Storm Drain is an asset rather than a hazard, which is why Huntail's set carries no single-target Water attack at all - Shell Smash into Double-Edge, Crunch and Ice Fang keeps it entirely out of the redirection matrix, and the Double-Edge recoil is the price of staying off the Water lane. Starmie's Analytic adds 30% damage whenever it moves last, which the Tailwind is deliberately not built to prevent. Could this team be cooler? The authored concept is one of the best ideas in the gym and stays exactly as it is - but it had a live defect its own prose flagged: Huntail's Waterfall was a single-target Water attack standing beside two Storm Drain allies, so the room's reserve regularly fed its own partner instead of attacking. Replacing it with Double-Edge makes Huntail a clean Shell Smash breaker with no Water attack at all, and it means the Surf lesson now works in every deployment rather than only the lead one. The memorable interaction - an opponent deliberately hitting its own partner to power it up - is preserved intact. Overrepresented? Lumineon's Storm Drain is unique to this room by design (Linda's route version is switched to Swift Swim to avoid exactly this defect); Gastrodon, Octillery and Starmie appear once each; Seaking's Lightning Rod is kept here and removed from the Seafloor grunt for the same redirection reason. Replacing it with Double-Edge makes Huntail a clean Shell Smash breaker with no Water attack at all, and it means the Surf lesson now works in every deployment rather than only the lead one. The memorable interaction - an opponent deliberately hitting its own partner to power it up - is preserved intact. Overrepresented? Lumineon's Storm Drain is unique to this room by design (Linda's route version is switched to Swift Swim to avoid exactly this defect); Gastrodon, Octillery and Starmie appear once each; Seaking's Lightning Rod is kept here and removed from the Seafloor grunt for the same redirection reason. Levels: cap 84, offsets 2/2/2/2/2/3.
weakest_link: Grass attacks ignore the whole redirection plan and hit both Storm Drain bodies for double damage. Wide Guard blanks Surf entirely, which shuts the engine off in one move. Taunt stops Tailwind and Recover; exploit Seaking's Choice lock; and Starmie is fast but extremely frail.

First two useful turns: Pelipper's Drizzle is live on entry, so Omastar is already fast; it opens with Tailwind, a U-turn pivot, or spread Muddy Water, and Omastar either attacks or takes a Shell Smash that White Herb immediately repairs. Turn two uses the real combined Swift Swim and Shell Smash speed rather than stacking further setup with no payoff. primary_question: Can the player beat this gym team (Carracosta, Araquanid, Cramorant, Tentacruel, Clawitzer, Blastoise) on its own terms: Concept: room six - the artillery room. Mega Launcher pulses, a Water Bubble spider that doubles its own Water damage, and a cormorant that spits its catch back at whoever hit it. First two useful turns: Carracosta takes a Shell Smash only when Araquanid's attack or Wide Guard buys a survivable window; unlike every other Shell Smash in the gym this one holds a Weakness Policy rather than a White Herb, so the Defence drops stay and the gamble is real - the payoff is that a super-effective hit raises both attacking stats by two more stages on top. Turn two uses the actual boosts and Policy state. Alternate deployment: Tentacruel's Liquid Ooze punishes Giga Drain, Leech Life and Draining Kiss by damaging the drainer instead of healing it, which is a specific and nasty answer to the Grass types brought to beat a Water gym; it fronts for Choice Specs Clawitzer, whose Mega Launcher raises every pulse move by half again. Reserves & disruption: Cramorant is the room's signature - after it uses Surf it holds a catch, and the next attacker to strike it takes damage and either a Defence drop or paralysis in return, whichever form it swallowed. Three of the six are immune to Water attacks, so Vaporeon's spread Surf is a full-power attack on both opposing slots that heals its own partner instead of hurting it. First two useful turns: Vaporeon Surfs while a Water Absorb partner stands beside it, gaining a free quarter of HP for that ally; Seismitoad or Mantine attacks in the other slot. Turn two sets Wish only when a real recipient will still be alive at the end of the following turn. Alternate deployment: Vaporeon's support enables Barbaracle's White Herb Shell Smash, but Surf is genuinely unsafe beside Barbaracle, so the AI must switch lanes rather than blindly repeat the engine - the lead pair and the setup pair are two separate modes. Reserves & disruption: Whiscash's Assault Vest physical line and Feraligatr's Sheer Force Dragon Dance are the non-absorbing finishers; Tough Claws boosts every contact move Barbaracle has, and Sheer Force removes Life Orb recoil on Feraligatr's Liquidation, Ice Punch and Crunch. Could this team be cooler? The Water Absorb Surf engine is a clean, teachable idea and the right seventh room, but the authored version only half-committed: Walrein's Choice-locked Blizzard was inaccurate with no snow anywhere in the gym, and the block's own prose admitted the partner matrix was unsafe. Moving Walrein to Daphne's ice room, where snow actually exists, and bringing Mantine in as a third Water Absorb body makes the engine genuinely dominant in its lead mode while keeping the honest cost that two members break it. That is a better fight than a room with six loosely related Water types. Overrepresented? Vaporeon's other owner is Hope in Victory Road with a Helping Hand support set; Mantine moves here from Crissy's room precisely so that absorption belongs to one room; Seismitoad's other owner Archie runs Swift Swim; Barbaracle, Feraligatr and Whiscash's Assault Vest set are unique here. Moving Walrein to Daphne's ice room, where snow actually exists, and bringing Mantine in as a third Water Absorb body makes the engine genuinely dominant in its lead mode while keeping the honest cost that two members break it. That is a better fight than a room with six loosely related Water types. Overrepresented? Vaporeon's other owner is Hope in Victory Road with a Helping Hand support set; Mantine moves here from Crissy's room precisely so that absorption belongs to one room; Seismitoad's other owner Archie runs Swift Swim; Barbaracle, Feraligatr and Whiscash's Assault Vest set are unique here. Levels: cap 84, offsets 2/2/2/2/2/3.

primary_question: Can the player beat this gym team (Palafin, Barraskewda, Azumarill, Greninja, Inteleon, Kingler) on its own terms: Concept: room eight - the strike team. This is the gym's speed-and-priority room: everything here either moves first or hits before the player can react. First two useful turns: Palafin leads and uses Flip Turn or a hard switch only when a healthy receiver exists, because leaving the field transforms it into Hero Form - on its second entry it is a different, far larger Pokemon with a Jet Punch that outspeeds everything. Barraskewda attacks beside it with Propeller Tail, which cannot be pulled away by Follow Me, Rage Powder or Storm Drain. Turn two commits to whichever of the two transformations or boosts actually landed. Alternate deployment: Azumarill's Belly Drum is admitted only after a survival check - it costs half its HP for a maximised Attack that Huge Power then doubles again, making Aqua Jet a priority attack with no realistic counterplay except killing it first. Reserves & disruption: Greninja's Protean changes its type to match each move as it uses it, so it is never the type the player prepared for; Sniper Inteleon converts its critical hits into removals; Mega Kingler is the closer, with Crabhammer's high critical rate behind it. Palafin's late placement must not strand an untransformed Hero with no reserve left to pivot into. Could this team be cooler? The Zero to Hero idea is the best single mechanic in the gym and stays as the room's spine, but the authored roster buried it: Dhelmise and Crawdaunt were slow bodies in a room about speed, and Mega Sharpedo made this the campaign's third owner of that exact stone after Archie and the Elite Four's Dark specialist. Rebuilding around Barraskewda, Greninja and Inteleon makes every slot serve the same idea, and Mega Kingler gives the room a Mega nobody else in the campaign fields. The memorable moment is the pivot itself - the player kills a modest dolphin and then meets Hero Form two turns later. Overrepresented? Mega Kingler, Palafin and Inteleon appear only here; Greninja's other owner is Felix's Mega version deep in Victory Road; Barraskewda's other owner is a Seafloor grunt with a Focus Sash; Azumarill's remaining owners are the route trainer Kara and nobody else, since Wally's Victory Road team is rebuilt to his canonical partners. Levels: cap 84, offsets 2/2/2/2/2/3.

ai_profile: sharp
primary_question: Can the player beat this gym team (Golduck, Quaquaval, Empoleon, Milotic, Basculegion, Samurott Hisui) on its own terms: Concept: room nine - the still room. Annika is the gym's contrarian: her Golduck's Cloud Nine switches off every weather effect in the building, including her own colleagues' rain, and the rest of her team is built to win without any. First two useful turns: Golduck attacks or takes a Nasty Plot while Quaquaval opens with Aqua Step, which raises its own Speed on every use and stacks with Moxie's Attack boost after each knockout - a self-accelerating sweeper that needs no weather at all. Turn two uses the real boosts rather than adding a third. Alternate deployment: Empoleon's Competitive doubles its Special Attack whenever any stat of its is lowered, so an opposing Intimidate, Snarl or Icy Wind hands it a free Nasty Plot; Assault Vest bulk lets it stay in for that. Reserves & disruption: Milotic's Flame Orb self-burn activates Marvel Scale for a 50% Defence boost at the cost of residual damage, and Hisuian Samurott's Sharpness sharply boosts its slicing moves while Ceaseless Edge lays Spikes on every hit. Basculegion is the Adaptability special closer. Note that Aqua Step is a dance, so an opposing Dancer copies it. Could this team be cooler? Yes, and it needed the change more than any other room except Brianna's. Pyukumuku's Counter-and-Toxic opening was pure passivity in a gym that is supposed to be eleven consecutive benchmarks, and the block's own prose flagged it for anti-passivity testing. Replacing it with Basculegion gives the room a real sixth threat, a Water/Ghost typing nothing else in the gym has, and an immunity to the Fighting and Normal attacks the player brings for Empoleon and Milotic. What remains is the room's genuinely distinctive idea - three different self-boosting mechanisms (Aqua Step, Moxie, Competitive) that all reward the player for attacking, so patience is punished and impatience is punished differently. Overrepresented? Quaquaval, Empoleon, Hisuian Samurott and Basculegion are unique in the campaign; Milotic's other owner is Champion Wallace's Mega; Golduck's Cloud Nine echoes the route sailor Hudson deliberately, as the player-side lesson resurfacing as an opponent. Levels: cap 84, offsets 2/2/2/2/2/3.

Walrein attacks beside it with Thick Fat cutting incoming Fire and Ice damage in half. Turn two uses the real weather state and picks between Blizzard's now-perfect accuracy and single-target damage. Alternate deployment: Cryogonal's Levitate makes it immune to Ground attacks, and its Icy Wind and Rapid Spin support Samurott's physical line. Reserves & disruption: snow makes Blizzard never miss, so Walrein's Choice Specs lock is far less dangerous than it looks once the weather is up; Rotom-Wash supplies the Electric coverage the room otherwise lacks and Levitate keeps it out of Ground range; Fur Coat halves physical damage against Dewgong. Could this team be cooler? It is now the room the gym was missing. The authored version had no engine at all - four unrelated Water types plus a Tapu Fini that duplicated Champion Wallace's own legend, which is exactly the kind of collision that makes a later fight feel less special. Rebuilding Daphne as the snow room gives Sootopolis its eleventh distinct strategy, hands Freeze-Dry to the one trainer for whom being a Water gym's worst matchup is the joke, and lets Walrein's Blizzard finally be accurate somewhere. Cryogonal is the rare, genuinely strange body the room deserves: a floating ice crystal with enormous Special Defence and no Ground weakness. Overrepresented? Cryogonal, Walrein and Dewgong appear only here in the gym; Lapras's other owners are the route trainer Everett's Perish Song set and Micah's Mega far into the post-game; Rotom-Wash recurs with Keira after the League. Tapu Fini is returned to Champion Wallace alone. Levels: cap 84, offsets 2/2/2/2/2/3.

ai_profile: master
primary_question: Can the player beat this leader team (Politoed, Suicune, Toxapex, Manaphy, Kingdra, Gyarados) on its own terms: Concept: the eleventh door - Juan takes the same rain his gym has been teaching and uses it for attrition rather than burst, then ends the fight with a Mega. Everything the ten rooms showed the player in isolation arrives here at once. First two useful turns: Politoed's Drizzle is live on entry with a Damp Rock behind it and opens with Encore to lock the player into a support move they have just wasted, or spread Muddy Water; Suicune picks Tailwind, Snarl or immediate pressure according to the board. Turn two must introduce a real attacker if the opening pair is being out-paced - Juan's failure mode is passivity and the plan explicitly forbids it. Alternate deployment: Suicune's control supports Manaphy's Tail Glow, which raises Special Attack by three stages in one turn and, under Hydration, is protected from any status the player tries to interrupt it with while the rain lasts. Reserves & disruption: Toxapex is the wall with a job - Wide Guard actively protects a partner from the spread attacks this roster invites, Acid Spray halves a target's Special Defence for a real follow-up, and Regenerator refunds a third of its HP on every switch. Choice Specs Swift Swim Kingdra is the burst reserve, doubling its Speed in the rain it did not have to set. Mega Gyarados is the closer and its Intimidate is deliberately spent before transformation. Could this team be cooler? This was already the strongest authored encounter in the range and the honest judgement is that it earns retention almost unchanged - the difference between Juan and Shelly's identical-looking rain team is that Shelly wants the fight over in four turns and Juan wants it to last twelve, and both are legible in play. The changes are about weight rather than concept: the leader was authored barely above his own gym trainers, so the offsets rise to place him a clear tier above all eleven rooms and above Archie, and the AI trait moves to Double Ace Pokemon so Manaphy and Mega Gyarados are both treated as finishers instead of one. Overrepresented? Politoed's Drizzle is shared with Shelly by design and with nobody else; Suicune, Manaphy and Mega Gyarados are unique to this fight; Kingdra's other owners are two route trainers at far lower tiers; Toxapex's other owner is a Seafloor grunt using Haze instead of Wide Guard. Levels: cap 84, offsets 3/3/3/4/4/5 - badge eight should cost the player its whole team.

primary_question: Can the player beat this regular team (Indeedee F, Hatterene, Reuniclus, Meowstic) on its own terms: Concept: a psychic quartet that turns its own terrain into a damage multiplier - Expanding Force becomes a spread attack with half again the power while Psychic Terrain is up, so three of the four are firing a boosted two-target move. First two useful turns: Indeedee-F establishes Psychic Surge on entry and redirects with Follow Me only when it preserves a worthwhile Expanding Force; Hatterene attacks. Turn two checks actual groundedness - the terrain and its priority-blocking effect only apply to grounded targets - and whether the terrain is still the team's own. Alternate deployment: Indeedee-F supports Reuniclus's Magic Guard coverage when Hatterene's typing is unfavourable; Magic Guard means Reuniclus takes no damage from Life Orb, burn, poison, hazards or sandstorm. Reserves & disruption: Hatterene's Magic Bounce reflects Taunt, Thunder Wave, Leech Seed and hazards straight back at the sender, so status is not the answer here. Mega Meowstic's screens and its form's ability transition are separate matters; base Prankster gives its screens priority but never makes Expanding Force a priority attack. Could this team be cooler? The terrain-plus-Expanding-Force stack is a real doubles engine and Magic Bounce is a genuine puzzle for a player who has been solving fights with Taunt, so this earns retention as a route regular. The block also carried a live legality error - Mega Meowstic was given Expanding Force, which it cannot learn - so its fourth slot becomes ordinary Psychic, which is honest and still benefits from the terrain. What would make it cooler is deliberately withheld: a Trick Room would turn it into a third room-team in a stretch that already has three, and the psychic-terrain identity is cleaner without one. Overrepresented? Indeedee-F recurs only with Wally's post-game rematch; Hatterene, Reuniclus and Mega Meowstic appear once each; Alexis is the only Psychic Terrain owner before the League. primary_question: Can the player beat this casual team (Starmie, Chimecho, Pikachu, Alakazam) on its own terms: Concept: a collector's parlour team - four famous faces, one of them wearing a Mega stone nobody expects to exist. First two useful turns: Starmie attacks with Natural Cure keeping it clean of status between switches while Chimecho chooses Helping Hand at a real threshold or its own Hyper Voice. Turn two uses the actual post-transformation ability rather than the base one. Alternate deployment: Pikachu's Fake Out buys Alakazam a turn of immediate Psychic pressure; Magic Guard means Alakazam ignores all indirect damage, so hazards and residual chip never break its Focus Sash. Reserves & disruption: the Light Ball doubles Pikachu's Attack and Special Attack for its attacks and does nothing for Fake Out's utility or its support turns; Encore requires observed move history to be worth the action. Could this team be cooler? It is the right size for a casual trainer and the honest answer is that the concept - a Mega Chimecho, of all things, standing beside a Light Ball Pikachu - is already more memorable than a stronger team would be, because it is the campaign's own invented Mega on the least likely species. Making it rarer or bulkier would remove the charm without adding difficulty the slot is meant to have. The change is confined to levels, so the fight is a brief real test rather than free experience. Overrepresented? Mega Chimecho and Light Ball Pikachu are unique in the campaign; Starmie's other owners are Connie's gym room and Champion Wallace's Mega; Alakazam appears once elsewhere. Levels: cap 90, offsets 0/0/0/1.

primary_question: Can the player beat this regular team (Lapras, Wobbuffet, Beheeyem, Musharna) on its own terms: Concept: the campaign's perish-trap prototype - Wobbuffet's Shadow Tag forbids the player from switching, Lapras starts a three-turn countdown, and both sides watch the clock. First two useful turns: Lapras uses Perish Song when Wobbuffet can hold the trap and both friendly slots still have a legal exit of their own; Wobbuffet Encores a committed move or waits with Counter and Mirror Coat, which return double the physical or special damage it just took. Turn two plays the countdown honestly - the trapper must leave or deliberately trade before it reaches zero, and switching the trapper releases the opponents early. Alternate deployment: Beheeyem and Musharna are the slower control fallback when the trap is answered - Analytic adds 30% to Beheeyem's damage whenever it moves last, which a Trick Room makes reliable. Reserves & disruption: Life Dew heals both allies, Safeguard blocks the status a trapped player reaches for, and Forewarn tells Musharna the strongest move on the opposing side. Wobbuffet is deliberately given no Protect - the script must not be made easy. Could this team be cooler? The perish trap is the rarest strategy in the campaign and appears exactly once, which is the right frequency; a second owner would make it a gimmick rather than an event. The block carried one legality error - Beheeyem cannot learn Helping Hand - so it becomes Energy Ball, which also gives the control half a real answer to the Ground and Water types that otherwise wall it. The honest limitation stays recorded: countdown ordering, simultaneous faints and escape sequencing are native acceptance gates, not assumptions. Overrepresented? Wobbuffet, Beheeyem and Musharna's Forewarn set are unique; Lapras's other owners are Daphne's gym ice room and Micah's post-game Mega. Levels: cap 90, offsets 0/1/1/1.

=== ENCOUNTER 0476 ===
physical_group_id: PHYSICAL_VICTORYROAD_1F_0046
proposed_encounter_id: PHYSICAL_VICTORYROAD_1F_0046
campaign_order: 476
atlas_ordinal: 476
chapter: Pokémon League
strict_cap: 80
location: VictoryRoad_1F
requirement: required
status: master_audited_ready_for_implementation
battle_class: rival
ai_profile: master
primary_question: Can the player beat this rival team (Delcatty, Gardevoir, Altaria, Magnezone, Roselia, Gallade) on its own terms: Concept: the rival arc, part one. This is Wally's own team - the partners he has actually raised since Petalburg - brought to Victory Road standard and crowned with the Mega he was always going to earn. First two useful turns: Delcatty opens with Fake Out to steal the player's first action, or Helping Hand when Gardevoir's Moonblast or Psychic is already lethal; Gardevoir attacks, with Trace having copied the most useful opposing ability the moment it entered. Turn two picks the reserve that answers whatever Trace revealed, and Heal Bell is spent only when a real status is crippling a real threat. Alternate deployment: Altaria's Tailwind and Roost line supports Magnezone, whose Magnet Pull traps the Steel types that wall the Fairy half of this team and removes them at leisure. Reserves & disruption: Eviolite Roselia is Wally's oldest partner and is genuinely bulky with it, landing Sleep Powder while Natural Cure keeps it clean; Mega Gallade's Sharpness sharply boosts Psycho Cut, Sacred Sword and Night Slash. Fake Out only works on the turn Delcatty enters, and Wonder Skin halves the accuracy of status moves aimed at it but does nothing against damage. Could this team be cooler? Yes, and this is the change the whole rival arc needed. The authored team was Garchomp, Togekiss and Azumarill - three Pokemon that belong to Cynthia and to route trainers, none of which Wally has ever owned - so the campaign's rival arrived at Victory Road as a generic good team with a Gallade attached. Rebuilding it from his actual line-up gives the player a fight they can read as a character: the Ralts from Petalburg is now a Gardevoir and a Mega Gallade standing side by side, the Roselia is still a Roselia, and the Delcatty that opened his original team is still the one buying the first turn. It is both cooler and more personal, and it removes the Cynthia collision three encounters from the end of the campaign. Overrepresented? Delcatty, Altaria and Roselia appear nowhere else; Magnezone's other owner is Wattson's gym far earlier; Gardevoir recurs only with Wally's own post-game rematch, where it becomes the Mega and Gallade steps back - a deliberate mirror. Togekiss is returned to Cynthia alone and Garchomp to Cynthia and Caroline. Levels: cap 90 incoming; his defeat is what raises the cap to 96, so the League tier is earned here. Offsets 1/2/1/1/1/3.

=== ENCOUNTER 0477 ===
physical_group_id: PHYSICAL_VICTORYROAD_1F_0102
proposed_encounter_id: PHYSICAL_VICTORYROAD_1F_0102
campaign_order: 477
atlas_ordinal: 477
chapter: Pokémon League
strict_cap: 80
location: VictoryRoad_1F
requirement: optional
status: master_audited_ready_for_implementation
battle_class: ace
ai_profile: sharp
primary_question: Can the player beat this ace team (Trevenant, Sudowoodo, Venomoth, Klinklang, Manectric, Hawlucha) on its own terms: Concept: the first door of Victory Road - a mechanical gauntlet where three separate members set up in three incompatible ways and the player cannot answer all of them. First two useful turns: Trevenant's Will-O-Wisp cripples a physical lead while Sudowoodo's Rock Head makes Head Smash entirely recoil-free, which is the hardest opening hit in this stretch; Natural Cure keeps Trevenant clean across switches. Turn two answers whichever setup the player failed to stop. Alternate deployment: Venomoth's Tinted Lens makes even resisted Bug Buzz and Sludge Bomb land at neutral damage, so a Quiver Dance behind a Focus Sash is a genuine sweep threat; Klinklang's Shift Gear doubles its Speed and raises Attack, and Clear Body refuses every stat drop the player aims at it. Reserves & disruption: Choice Scarf Manectric with Lightning Rod is the emergency speed control and Electric absorber; Mega Hawlucha's Mold Breaker ignores abilities entirely, so Sturdy, Levitate and Water Absorb do not save anything from Close Combat or Brave Bird. Could this team be cooler? The three-setup structure is the right identity for the gauntlet's opening gate, and the Mold Breaker Mega is a genuinely good closer because it invalidates exactly the defensive abilities a player leans on after eleven Water rooms. It earns retention. The improvement it needed was tier: authored at flat offsets it read as a route ace that had wandered into Victory Road, so the whole team rises and Mega Hawlucha rises further. Tinted Lens Venomoth is the member worth defending - it is the only thing in the range that makes resistances irrelevant, and that is a better kind of pressure than raw stats. Overrepresented? Trevenant, Sudowoodo, Venomoth, Klinklang and Mega Hawlucha are unique in the campaign; Manectric's other owner is the post-game ship trainer Micah, whose duplicate Scarf set is replaced in this pass. Reserves & disruption: Choice Scarf Manectric with Lightning Rod is the emergency speed control and Electric absorber; Mega Hawlucha's Mold Breaker ignores abilities entirely, so Sturdy, Levitate and Water Absorb do not save anything from Close Combat or Brave Bird. Could this team be cooler? primary_question: Can the player beat this ace team (Rhyperior, Sableye, Weavile, Ursaluna, Guzzlord, Glimmora) on its own terms: Concept: the control gate - no weather, no terrain, just a Prankster that decides the turn order and five very heavy bodies behind it. First two useful turns: Sableye's priority Fake Out, Quash or Encore rearranges the turn before it happens - Quash in particular forces a fast opposing attacker to move last, which is what makes the slow half of this team work. Rhyperior attacks, holding a Weakness Policy behind Solid Rock, which reduces super-effective damage by a quarter and therefore makes surviving the hit that triggers the Policy far likelier. Turn two cashes whichever advantage the control turn bought. Alternate deployment: Weavile's Pressure and Knock Off strip items while Guzzlord's Beast Boost turns each knockout into more Attack; Guzzlord's absurd HP makes it the one thing here that survives a full-power special attack. Reserves & disruption: Ursaluna's Flame Orb Guts converts a burn into a damage bonus and Headlong Rush is the single heaviest Ground attack in the range; Mega Glimmora's Toxic Debris scatters Toxic Spikes whenever it is hit by a physical attack, so attacking it physically poisons the player's own grounded team. Could this team be cooler? The Quash-plus-Solid-Rock-Policy interaction is a real, unusual plan and Mega Glimmora is a genuinely memorable Mega, so the concept holds. The change made is to Conkeldurr, which was an exact duplicate of Mitchell's set seven doors later in the same gauntlet: Ursaluna is rarer, hits harder, fits the same Guts-and-Flame-Orb role, and gives the gauntlet a Ground attacker that Trick Room teams later in the road can be compared against. That turns a repeated slot into the fight's second-scariest body. Overrepresented? Turn two brings the member that punishes whatever the player committed to. Alternate deployment: Salazzle's Corrosion lets it poison Steel and Poison types that believe they are immune, which is a specific answer to the Steel walls this team otherwise cannot break; Aerodactyl's Tailwind and Taunt handle the speed race. Reserves & disruption: Vaporeon's Muddy Water is spread, so it cannot be stolen by its own Storm Drain ace, and Helping Hand is its real job; Mega Tatsugiri's Storm Drain draws every opposing single-target Water attack and converts it into a Special Attack boost, which is the team's signature - a player who leads with Water hands the sweeper a free stage before it even acts. Could this team be cooler? The shape is right and unusual: five support-shaped bodies and one tiny, absurd Mega sushi dragon that ends the game. It earns retention. The block's one real risk is that the Storm Drain bait only works if the player brings Water, so the redundancy matters - Nasty Plot means Tatsugiri can boost itself when nobody obliges. The improvement made is tier and pacing: at flat offsets the support turns were free for the player, so everything rises and the Mega rises further, making the two-turn setup an actual race. physical_group_id: PHYSICAL_VICTORYROAD_1F_0117
proposed_encounter_id: PHYSICAL_VICTORYROAD_1F_0117
campaign_order: 480

status: master_audited_ready_for_implementation
battle_class: ace
ai_profile: sharp
primary_question: Can the player beat this ace team (Slaking, Weezing, Butterfree, Durant, Terrakion, Zygarde 50 Power Construct) on its own terms: Concept: the cleverest single idea in Victory Road - a team built entirely around turning off the worst ability in the game. Slaking has Truant and can only attack every other turn; Weezing's Neutralizing Gas suppresses every ability on the field while it is alive, Truant included, so a Choice Scarf Slaking with 160 base Attack simply attacks every turn instead. The authored SUPPRESS tactic is what tells the AI to keep Weezing alive for exactly that reason. First two useful turns: Weezing enters beside Slaking and stays; Slaking fires Double-Edge or High Horsepower with no downtime. Turn two protects the suppressor - the moment Weezing dies, Slaking loses half its turns. Alternate deployment: Durant's Entrainment is the backup plan and the fight's second joke - it forcibly gives Truant to an opposing Pokemon, locking the player's own sweeper out of every other turn. Butterfree's Compound Eyes makes Sleep Powder effectively accurate and Rage Powder protects the suppressor. Reserves & disruption: Terrakion's Quick Guard blocks the priority aimed at Weezing; Mega Zygarde's Thousand Arrows hits even airborne targets and grounds them, and Power Construct is suppressed while Weezing lives, which is a real cost the AI must weigh. Glare paralyses regardless of type. Could this team be cooler? No - this is the best-designed encounter in the range and it is kept intact. Every slot serves one absurd, legible idea, the player can beat it by killing a Weezing, and doing so visibly halves the boss's output; the Entrainment mirror means the trick can be turned on the player as well. The only change is tier, so that the Slaking turns actually hurt while the player is solving the puzzle. Worth noting for the AI audit: Neutralizing Gas suppressing the team's own Power Construct is a genuine tension and the tactic line must not be read as an instruction to Mega at all costs. Overrepresented? Slaking, Weezing, Durant, Butterfree, Terrakion and Mega Zygarde appear nowhere else in the campaign; this is the only Neutralizing Gas or Entrainment owner. Levels: cap 96, offsets 1/1/1/1/1/2.
theme_and_tempo: Concept: the cleverest single idea in Victory Road - a team built entirely around turning off the worst ability in the game. Slaking has Truant and can only attack every other turn; Weezing's Neutralizing Gas suppresses every ability on the field while it is alive, Truant included, so a Choice Scarf Slaking with 160 base Attack simply attacks every turn instead. The authored SUPPRESS tactic is what tells the AI to keep Weezing alive for exactly that reason. Turn two protects the suppressor - the moment Weezing dies, Slaking loses half its turns. First two useful turns: Audino's Regenerator bulk lets it Wish or Helping Hand while Infernape's Fake Out and mixed Naive spread buy the turn; Wish pays out at the end of the following turn to whoever is in the slot, so it must be aimed at a body that will still be there. Turn two commits to the damage the support turn bought. Alternate deployment: Bewear's Fluffy halves contact damage while doubling Fire damage taken, which is a real and specific weakness in a Fire team; Choice Specs Victini with Victory Star raises the accuracy of every move on its own side by 10%, so the team's Heat Waves, Overheats and Focus Blasts are all steadier while it is out. Alternate deployment: Orbeetle's Light Screen and Telepathy mode is the patient build, with Telepathy making it immune to its partner's own spread attacks; Goodra's Assault Vest bulk gives the team a special sponge it otherwise lacks, and Gooey lowers the Speed of anything that makes contact with it, so the physical attackers brought to break it end up slower than the Tailwind team every turn they connect. Reserves & disruption: Vikavolt's Levitate and Choice Specs make it a Ground-immune artillery piece that punishes the Water and Flying answers brought for Emboar; Sawsbuck's Sap Sipper turns an opposing Grass attack into a free Attack boost. Reckless raises Flare Blitz, Head Smash and Double-Edge but not Drain Punch, and all three hurt Emboar badly. Could this team be cooler? The early-Mega structure is a genuine change of rhythm in a gauntlet where every other trainer saves the transformation for last, so it stays. Two slots changed for duplication rather than taste: Escavalier's Bug Gem set was a copy of Marley's route ace and Dragonite duplicated both Aaron's Mega and Drake's League ace, so Vikavolt and Goodra replace them. Both are rarer, both cover a hole the original pair did not - Ground immunity and a contact-punishing special wall - and neither repeats a set the player has already solved. Overrepresented? Vikavolt, Goodra, Ribombee, Orbeetle and Mega Emboar are unique in the campaign after this pass; Sawsbuck's other owner is Jonathan far earlier with a Clear Amulet. Levels: cap 96, offsets 1/2/1/1/1/1.

battle_class: ace
ai_profile: sharp
primary_question: Can the player beat this ace team (Meganium, Machamp, Chansey, Hydreigon, Probopass, Umbreon) on its own terms: Concept: the wall. Michelle is Victory Road's attrition gate - a Mega Meganium whose Triage gives Heal Pulse priority, a Chansey behind an Eviolite, and three bodies that simply refuse to die on schedule. First two useful turns: Mega Meganium uses Heal Pulse, which restores half a partner's HP and, through Triage, does so before almost anything on the field can act - so the player must out-damage a full heal every turn, not merely out-damage a Pokemon. Machamp attacks beside it with No Guard making Dynamic Punch a guaranteed hit and a guaranteed confusion. Turn two chooses between another heal and Light Screen depending on which damage type is actually killing. Alternate deployment: Chansey's Seismic Toss deals fixed damage that ignores every defensive stat, and Soft-Boiled keeps it there; Umbreon's Foul Play uses the target's own Attack, so it punishes exactly the physical sweeper a player brings to break walls. Reserves & disruption: Hydreigon is the one genuinely fast special attacker and the answer to a player who has switched to passive play; Probopass's Magnet Pull traps Steel types and Stealth Rock taxes every switch this team is trying to force. Could this team be cooler? The Triage Heal Pulse idea is excellent and rare, and a pure stall gate is the right change of pace in a gauntlet of sweepers, so the concept holds. The change is Tyranitar, which set sand for a team with no sand abusers at all and duplicated Caroline's dedicated sand team five doors later - a mislabelled strategy flag and a collision in one slot. Umbreon replaces it with a body that actually belongs in a stall team, adds a Dark type to a roster that had no answer to Psychic and Ghost attackers, and makes Foul Play the trap that punishes the player's obvious counterplay. The SAND flag is corrected to SETUP. Overrepresented? Umbreon, Meganium, Machamp, Chansey and Hydreigon are unique in the campaign; Probopass's other owner is Susie's route team; Tyranitar is returned to Caroline alone. Levels: cap 96, offsets 2/1/1/1/1/1.

primary_question: Can the player beat this ace team (Shiinotic, Gothitelle, Conkeldurr, Scovillain, Marowak Alola, Reuniclus) on its own terms: Concept: Victory Road's Trick Room gate, and the one that traps you inside it - Gothitelle's Shadow Tag means the reversed order is not something you can simply switch out of. First two useful turns: Shiinotic's Spore puts a legal target to sleep with certainty while Gothitelle sets Trick Room; Effect Spore additionally inflicts a random status on anything that makes contact with Shiinotic, and Strength Sap drains the target's Attack while healing by that amount. Turn two spends the reversed order on damage. Alternate deployment: Guts Conkeldurr and Thick Club Alolan Marowak are the heavy mode - the Thick Club doubles Marowak's Attack, and Lightning Rod makes it the team's Electric absorber and a redirector against single-target Electric attacks. Reserves & disruption: Mega Scovillain's Insomnia keeps it awake beside its own Spore user, and its dual Grass and Fire special attacks cover the Water and Steel types brought against the room; Magic Guard Reuniclus takes no Life Orb recoil at all, which is why it can afford the item at this tier. All five slow members carry zero Speed IVs so the room works for them and not against them. Could this team be cooler? The trap-plus-room pairing is the right identity for this door, and Mega Scovillain is a genuinely strange, memorable ace. The improvement made is the same one the earlier room teams needed: every Brave, Quiet and Relaxed member now has a zero Speed IV, which is the difference between a Trick Room team and a team carrying the move. The Conkeldurr duplication with Albert is resolved on Albert's side rather than here, because Guts under Trick Room is the more natural home for the set. Overrepresented? Shiinotic, Alolan Marowak and Mega Scovillain are unique; Gothitelle recurs with the route ace Conor at a much lower tier, reading as escalation; Reuniclus's other owner is Alexis with an Assault Vest support role. Levels: cap 96, offsets 1/1/1/2/1/1.

battle_class: ace
ai_profile: sharp
primary_question: Can the player beat this ace team (Pinsir, Pachirisu, Lickilicky, Naganadel, Zarude, Falinks) on its own terms: Concept: a redirection-and-snowball door. Pachirisu holds the field while two very different self-boosters build, and the Mega closer boosts all five of its own stats in a single turn. First two useful turns: Pachirisu's Follow Me pulls single-target attacks off Pinsir, and Nuzzle guarantees paralysis on a target rather than gambling; Pinsir's Mold Breaker means Sturdy, Levitate, Water Absorb and Volt Absorb do nothing to stop its attacks. Turn two uses whichever body the redirection kept alive. Alternate deployment: Naganadel's Beast Boost raises its Special Attack after every knockout, so a Nasty Plot plus one kill is usually the end of the fight; Zarude is the immediate physical option with Knock Off stripping items. Reserves & disruption: Lickilicky's Cloud Nine suppresses every weather effect on the field, which is a specific answer to the sun, sand and snow teams either side of it in the gauntlet, and its single-use Normal Gem makes one Body Slam far larger than it looks. Mega Falinks's No Retreat raises Attack, Defence, Special Attack, Special Defence and Speed by one stage each at the cost of being unable to switch out - an all-in that the player can answer by simply surviving it. Could this team be cooler? It is already an unusually well-varied door: two Ultra-Beast-tier boosters, a legendary monkey, a redirector and the campaign's only Mega Falinks, with no shared weather or terrain to exploit. It earns retention. The honest criticism is that Pachirisu duplicates Brawly's gym support from very early in the campaign, but that is deliberate escalation rather than repetition - the same tiny squirrel, now protecting something that ends games - and replacing it would cost the fight its one memorable callback. The change is tier only. Overrepresented? Naganadel, Zarude, Lickilicky and Mega Falinks are unique in the campaign; Pinsir's Mega is owned elsewhere but this base Mold Breaker version is not; Pachirisu's only other owner is Brawly. Levels: cap 96, offsets 1/1/1/1/1/2.

primary_question: Can the player beat this ace team (Bisharp, Ninetales, Dodrio, Lurantis, Flygon, Raichu) on its own terms: Concept: the sun door - Drought on entry, Solar Beam with no charge turn, a Contrary Grass type that gets stronger every time it uses its strongest move, and a Mega Raichu X to close. First two useful turns: Ninetales establishes sun on entry and either fires an instantly charged Solar Beam or Encores a wasted opposing action; Bisharp attacks, and its Defiant means any stat drop aimed at it - an Intimidate, a Snarl, an Icy Wind - raises its Attack by two stages instead. Turn two uses the sun rather than reinforcing it. Alternate deployment: Lurantis's Contrary turns Leaf Storm's Special Attack drop into a two-stage raise, so it snowballs by attacking, and Superpower makes it physically tougher each time; Synthesis restores two-thirds of its HP under sun instead of half. Reserves & disruption: Choice Band Dodrio with Early Bird shrugs off sleep in a single turn, and Flygon's Yache Berry cushions the Ice attack that is otherwise its death; Mega Raichu X's Fake Out and Knock Off give the closer utility as well as damage. Could this team be cooler? The Contrary Lurantis and Defiant Bisharp pairing is the fight's real identity: both members are rewarded for the things a player normally does to weaken a team, which makes this door punish reflexive play rather than bad play. That earns retention and is why Lurantis stays here rather than with the route ace Sophia, who is rebuilt around a Dancer engine instead. The one duplication left is Bisharp against Dianne five doors later, and that is resolved on Dianne's side by promoting hers to Kingambit, so this remains the campaign's only Defiant Bisharp. Overrepresented? Mega Raichu X, Dodrio, Flygon and Lurantis are unique after this pass; Ninetales's Drought recurs only with Leaf's Kanto team in the post-game and with Maxie's Magma team far earlier, all with different payloads. Levels: cap 96, offsets 1/1/1/1/1/2.
