primary_question: Can the player beat this ace team (Tyranitar, Stoutland, Garchomp, Sandslash, Dugtrio Alola, Eternatus) on its own terms: Concept: the sandstorm door, and the only one in the gauntlet - five bodies that either double their Speed in sand, gain power from it, or are simply immune to its chip damage. First two useful turns: Tyranitar's Sand Stream is live on entry and Smooth Rock stretches it to eight turns, so Stoutland and Sandslash are already at doubled Speed before the player's lead acts; Tyranitar attacks or Protects to bank a turn. Turn two spends the Sand Rush window on damage, because the whole plan expires with the weather. Alternate deployment: Mega Garchomp arrives in the third slot rather than the last, which is deliberate - its Sand Veil raises evasion in the storm it is standing in, so it is hardest to remove exactly while the sand is up. Alolan Dugtrio's Sand Force raises its Ground, Rock and Steel attacks by 30% in sand, and Sucker Punch gives the team priority. Reserves & disruption: Eternatus is the weather-independent closer with Dynamax Cannon, Pressure doubling the PP cost of every move aimed at it, and enormous HP; it is the answer to a player who solves the sand and then expects the fight to be over. Could this team be cooler? It is the correct sand team for this position and the composition holds - three distinct sand abilities and a legendary that does not care about the weather is a genuinely good structure, and Sand Veil placed early rather than late is a smart, slightly unfair touch. The duplication with Michelle's mislabelled SAND flag five doors earlier is resolved on her side, so Caroline is now the campaign's only Sand Stream owner outside the Magma arc and the sandstorm reads as this trainer's signature. The remaining fix here was a legality error: Stoutland cannot learn Double-Edge, so it takes Retaliate instead, which doubles in power after an ally has fainted - a better fit for a team that expects to trade. Overrepresented? Stoutland, Alolan Dugtrio, Sandslash and Eternatus are unique in the campaign; Mega Garchomp recurs only as Cynthia's custom Garchomp Z variant in the final optional fight, a deliberate mirror; Tyranitar's other owners are the Magma arc far earlier. primary_question: Can the player beat this ace team (Torkoal, Venusaur, Heliolisk, Lycanroc, Zamazenta, Victreebel) on its own terms: Concept: the second sun door, deliberately built the opposite way round to Vito's - his sun powers a Contrary snowballer, hers powers two Chlorophyll sweepers and a Solar Power glass cannon. First two useful turns: Torkoal's Drought is live on entry and Eruption fires at full power only while Torkoal is at full HP, so the player must damage it before it acts; Venusaur is already at doubled Speed from Chlorophyll and opens with Sleep Powder or Giga Drain. Turn two uses the real HP and speed state rather than the opening one. Alternate deployment: Heliolisk's Solar Power raises its Special Attack by half in sun at the cost of HP every turn, and Glare paralyses regardless of the target's type; Lycanroc's Accelerock is the priority that punishes a weakened lead. Reserves & disruption: Zamazenta's Dauntless Shield raises its Defence on entry, and Iron Defence plus Body Press turns that defence directly into damage - a defensive legend inside an all-out sun team is a deliberate change of gear; Mega Victreebel's Weather Ball becomes a 100-power Fire attack under its own sun. Could this team be cooler? Two sun teams inside sixteen doors is a real question, and the answer is that they are legitimately different fights - Vito's rewards you for not weakening him, Julie's punishes you for not being fast - so both hold. What makes Julie's memorable is the Zamazenta slot: a player who has correctly brought a Water or Rock answer to a sun team then runs into a wall that gets tougher every turn and converts that toughness into damage. That contrast is worth more than a rarer sixth Fire type would be. The change here is tier only, plus the Victreebel duplication being resolved on Owen's side so the Mega is unique. Overrepresented? Heliolisk, Lycanroc, Zamazenta and Mega Victreebel are unique in the campaign; Torkoal and Venusaur recur at lower tiers with Darcy, Flannery and Marley in different ability roles. primary_question: Can the player beat this ace team (Jynx, Xerneas, Sceptile, Duraludon, Greninja, Aegislash) on its own terms: Concept: the last non-rival door before the League, and the only one that opens with sleep and closes with a stance change - six threats with no engine except raw quality. First two useful turns: Jynx's Lovely Kiss or Fake Out steals the opening turn while Xerneas, holding a Power Herb, uses Geomancy - a two-turn move that the Herb completes instantly, raising Special Attack, Special Defence and Speed by two stages each in a single turn. Turn two is the player's last chance to stop a fully set-up Fairy Aura legend. Alternate deployment: Sceptile and Mega Greninja are the fast mixed-attacking mode, with Protean changing Greninja's type to match each move it uses so its STAB is always live and its resistances are never the ones you prepared for. Reserves & disruption: Eviolite Duraludon is a genuine special wall because it still evolves, and Stalwart means its attacks cannot be redirected by Follow Me, Rage Powder or Storm Drain; Aegislash's Stance Change flips it to Blade Forme when it attacks and back to Shield Forme when it uses King's Shield, and its Weakness Policy means a super-effective hit while it is shielded makes the next attack enormous. Could this team be cooler? This is the correct final gate: one instant setup, one type-shifting Mega, one stance-shifting Policy closer, and a Stalwart wall that specifically defeats the redirection strategies the gauntlet has been teaching the player to use. It earns retention unchanged in composition. The one thing worth stating plainly is that Geomancy through Power Herb is the single most dangerous turn in Victory Road, and the level spread now reflects that the fight is meant to be decided on turn one or two. Overrepresented? Jynx, Xerneas, Duraludon, Aegislash and Mega Greninja are unique in the campaign; Sceptile's other owner is Susie's route team with a White Herb Unburden set; Greninja's base form appears once in the Sootopolis gym at a far lower tier. The one thing worth stating plainly is that Geomancy through Power Herb is the single most dangerous turn in Victory Road, and the level spread now reflects that the fight is meant to be decided on turn one or two. Overrepresented? Jynx, Xerneas, Duraludon, Aegislash and Mega Greninja are unique in the campaign; Sceptile's other owner is Susie's route team with a White Herb Unburden set; Greninja's base form appears once in the Sootopolis gym at a far lower tier. Levels: cap 96, offsets 1/2/1/1/2/1.
weakest_link: Stop Geomancy or lose. Deny Lovely Kiss with your own Fake Out, or lead with a Fire, Rock or Steel body that survives Jynx. Poison and Steel attacks answer Xerneas; Fighting and Ground answer Aegislash while it is in Blade Forme; and do not hit Aegislash super-effectively while it is shielded. Fighting and Ground answer Duraludon despite the Eviolite.

First two useful turns: Abomasnow's Snow Warning is live on entry, so Froslass can immediately use Aurora Veil, which needs snow to work at all and then reduces physical and special damage for five turns; Abomasnow's Blizzard never misses in its own weather. Turn two attacks from behind the veil rather than adding more setup. Alternate deployment: Magmortar and Virizion are the deliberately off-type answers to the Fire, Steel and Fighting attacks a player brings to beat an Ice team; Justified raises Virizion's Attack whenever a Dark attack hits it. Reserves & disruption: Froslass's Destiny Bond takes the attacker down with it, so removing the veil-setter has a real price; Kingambit's Supreme Overlord raises its Attack for every ally that has already fainted, which makes it strongest exactly when the fight is nearly over, and Sucker Punch turns that accumulated power into priority. Mega Barbaracle's Shell Smash under a still-active Aurora Veil is the intended finish. Could this team be cooler? === ENCOUNTER 0498 ===
physical_group_id: PHYSICAL_VICTORYROAD_1F_0089
proposed_encounter_id: PHYSICAL_VICTORYROAD_1F_0089
campaign_order: 498
atlas_ordinal: 498
chapter: Postgame Victory Road exhibition
strict_cap: 100
location: VictoryRoad_1F
requirement: optional
rematch_policy: first_campaign_encounter_only; later Match Call tiers excluded
status: master_audited_ready_for_implementation
battle_class: rival
ai_profile: master
primary_question: Can the player beat this rival team (Indeedee F, Gallade, Gardevoir, Tapu Lele, Magearna, Altaria) on its own terms: Concept: the rival arc, part two. Wally comes back as Champion-tier and the arc completes its mirror - the Gallade that was his Mega at Victory Road now stands beside him as an ordinary partner while Altaria, the Swablu he caught on Route 114, carries the stone. First two useful turns: Indeedee-F sets Psychic Terrain on entry and redirects with Follow Me to keep Gallade's Sharpness-boosted Psycho Cut or Sacred Sword alive; Psychic Terrain also blocks all priority moves aimed at his grounded members, which is what makes the setup viable at this level. Gallade attacks. Turn two picks the special half rather than repeating the redirect. Alternate deployment: Tapu Lele is the raw damage mode - its Psychic Surge re-establishes the terrain if it has been replaced, and under it Psychic and Psyshock hit half again as hard. Gardevoir's Trace copies the most valuable ability on the opposing side the moment it enters. Reserves & disruption: Magearna's Soul-Heart raises its Special Attack every time any Pokemon on the field faints, so a long fight makes it progressively lethal, and Fleur Cannon is enormous at the cost of a two-stage drop each use. Mega Altaria's Pixilate converts Return into a Fairy-type attack with a power bonus, and at maximum friendship Return is already at full power - a Dragon Dance behind that is the closer, and its Dragon/Fairy typing means the Steel answer the player saved for Magearna is the only thing that also answers this. Note that Psychic Terrain blocks the team's own priority as well, so Gallade has no safe priority option while it is up. Could this team be cooler? Yes, and the rebuild is what makes the two Wally fights a rival arc rather than two unrelated bosses. The new version keeps a single coherent Psychic and Fairy identity across both fights, promotes his own Altaria to the Mega slot using the campaign's one unused Altarianite, and makes the memorable moment structural: the player recognises every Pokemon, and the one that was a support in the first fight is now the thing that kills them. First two useful turns: Klefki's Prankster gives Thunder Wave, Light Screen and Foul Play priority, so the speed control lands before anything else happens, and its Steel/Fairy typing walls the Dragon and Dark attacks the rest of the team invites; Mienshao attacks and U-turns out, restoring a third of its HP through Regenerator each time it leaves. Turn two pivots only when the replacement genuinely improves the board. Alternate deployment: Poison Heal Gliscor is the independent Swords Dance mode - the Toxic Orb heals it every turn instead of damaging it, so it is immune to further status and gains HP while setting up. Reserves & disruption: Xurkitree's Beast Boost and Electroweb combine speed control with a Special Attack that grows after each knockout; Choice Scarf Typhlosion's Eruption is calculated from its current HP at the moment it fires, so it must come in clean. primary_question: Can the player beat this ace team (Gigalith, Sandslash, Whimsicott, Rotom Wash, Necrozma, Clefable) on its own terms: Concept: a sandstorm that exists to protect a single reactive nuke. Necrozma holds a Weakness Policy, and everything else on the team decides whether the player is allowed to trigger it. First two useful turns: Gigalith's Sand Stream is live on entry with a Smooth Rock behind it, so Sandslash is already at doubled Speed; Sandslash attacks. Turn two either spends the sand window or transitions to support - but only when that protects a body worth protecting. Alternate deployment: Clefable's Follow Me pulls a single-target attack away from Necrozma, which is a genuine decision rather than a free action, because a super-effective hit landing on Necrozma would raise both its attacking stats by two stages through the Policy - the redirection can correctly prevent the team's own payoff, and both benefits must never be counted at once. Prism Armor separately reduces super-effective damage against it by a quarter, making the Policy far likelier to fire safely. Reserves & disruption: Whimsicott's Prankster Tailwind and Encore are the backup speed plan for when the sand is replaced, not automatic redundancy; Rotom-Wash covers Water and Electric and takes sand chip every turn, which is a real cost. Mega Clefable is the closer. Could this team be cooler? The plan's internal tension - a redirector that can accidentally disarm its own ace - is unusually sophisticated and is exactly the kind of decision the AI audit should care about, so the concept earns retention unchanged. The honest note is that this is the second sand team in the post-game and the third overall; it is kept because its sand is a shield for a reactive item rather than a Sand Rush speed engine like Caroline's, which makes it a different fight despite the shared weather. Levels rise to post-game tier. Overrepresented? primary_question: Can the player beat this ace team (Liepard, Fezandipiti, Persian Alola, Incineroar, Mesprit, Floette Eternal) on its own terms: Concept: a cruise-liner cat burglar's team - Prankster control, two pivots and a tiny Fairy that quietly becomes unkillable. First two useful turns: Liepard's Prankster gives Fake Out, Taunt, Encore and Foul Play priority, so it takes the first turn and decides what the player is allowed to do with theirs; Fezandipiti attacks or sets Tailwind, and its Toxic Chain has a chance to badly poison on every hit. Turn two converts the control into damage rather than adding another passive support. Alternate deployment: Mesprit's Helping Hand and Thunder Wave behind a Covert Cloak - which blocks all secondary effects and Fake Out aimed at it - supports Mega Floette's Calm Mind. Reserves & disruption: Alolan Persian's Fur Coat halves physical damage and Foul Play uses the attacker's own Attack, so the pair of them punish physical setup twice over; Incineroar is the Intimidate pivot with Parting Shot lowering both of a target's attacking stats as it leaves. Eternal Floette's Flower Veil protects the team's Grass and Fairy members from stat drops, and Wish needs a recipient that will survive to receive it. Could this team be cooler? The composition is a good, thematically tight "thieves on a ship" roster and the four-way priority-control opening is genuinely oppressive, so it earns retention. Eternal Floette deserves specific defence: it is one of the rarest forms in the series, it is not simply a stat upgrade, and pairing its Calm Mind with Flower Veil and Wish makes it a win condition the player has to break through rather than out-damage. The change is tier - the block's stale note about a discarded level-100 floor is replaced by honest live-cap offsets. Overrepresented? Liepard, Fezandipiti, Alolan Persian, Mesprit and Mega Floette are unique in the campaign; Incineroar's other owners are the Elite Four's Dark specialist and Wally's earlier authored draft, which this pass removes. primary_question: Can the player beat this regular team (Weavile, Armarouge, Genesect, Scolipede) on its own terms: Concept: the deliberate friendly-fire combo - Weavile shoots its own partner on purpose. Armarouge has Weak Armor, so taking a physical hit lowers its Defence by one stage and raises its Speed by two; a resisted Ice Shard from a zero-Attack Weavile is the cheapest possible way to buy that boost. First two useful turns: the authored tactic fires Ice Shard into Armarouge only when the resisted damage and the Defence drop are genuinely worth the Speed, and Armarouge must not Protect through the trigger; Armarouge then attacks with Armor Cannon, which is enormous and lowers its own defences further. Turn two plays the real speed and survival state, not an imagined item boost. Alternate deployment: Weavile's Fake Out supports Choice Scarf Genesect's immediate special pressure with no friendly damage at all, which is the mode to use when Armarouge cannot afford the hit; Download raises Genesect's Attack or Special Attack on entry depending on which of the opposing defences is weaker. Reserves & disruption: Mega Scolipede's Speed Boost must be earned before transforming, and it is a separate timed plan rather than part of the combo. Weavile's Attack IV is deliberately zero to minimise the activation damage, which is a real cost to its Knock Off. Could this team be cooler? The activation combo is one of the campaign's most distinctive authored ideas and is kept exactly as designed - a trainer whose plan is to hurt their own Pokemon is memorable precisely because it looks like a mistake. The previously flagged amendment is applied here: the zero Attack IV is now in the set rather than only in the prose, so the combo is survivable as described. The one honest limitation recorded is that native survival and ordering tests are still required; this is an executable plan, not a proven one. Overrepresented? Armarouge, Genesect and Mega Scolipede are unique in the campaign; Weavile's other owner is Albert in Victory Road with a full-Attack Clear Amulet set, which is deliberately the opposite build. Levels: cap 100, offsets 0/1/1/1.

primary_question: Can the player beat this casual team (Miltank, Tauros, Primeape, Bouffalant) on its own terms: Concept: a ranch couple's herd - four heavy Normal and Fighting bodies, no gimmick, and one of them hitting far harder than a casual slot suggests. First two useful turns: Miltank uses Helping Hand only when Tauros's Double-Edge or Close Combat actually crosses a threshold, and Body Slam otherwise - Scrappy lets it hit Ghost types that expect an immunity. Tauros attacks after its own Intimidate has softened the lead. Turn two may bring Primeape, whose Defiant turns any stat drop aimed at it into a two-stage Attack raise. Alternate deployment: Bouffalant and Primeape are the pure aggression mode - Reckless raises Head Charge and Megahorn, at a recoil cost Bouffalant's HP can afford. Reserves & disruption: Milk Drink restores half Miltank's HP and is the herd's only recovery; Choice Band Bouffalant is locked once it commits. Could this team be cooler? It is cooler than it was, for a legality reason as well as a design one. The authored fourth slot was a Cosmog with Double-Edge and Teleport - a charming idea, but Cosmog cannot learn Double-Edge at all, so the set was illegal and the slot was in practice a two-move Pokemon that could not fight. Bouffalant replaces it with something that genuinely belongs on a ranch, is rarely seen anywhere in the series, and gives the pair a fourth real threat so the fight is a fight. The novelty is not lost - a Choice Band Head Charge from a woolly bull is its own kind of joke - and the encounter no longer depends on a form whose attack legality could not be validated. Overrepresented? Bouffalant, Tauros and Primeape are unique in the campaign; Miltank's other owner is the route trainer Kara far earlier with the same Scrappy identity, which is the intended echo for a pair of ranchers. Levels: cap 100, offsets 0/1/1/1.

First two useful turns: Tsareena attacks or pivots while Salazzle uses Fake Out only when it buys a useful action; Queenly Majesty blocks all opposing priority moves aimed at Naomi's side, which is specifically what protects the setup turn that follows. Turn two can introduce Darkrai once the opening is safe. Alternate deployment: Salazzle's Corrosion lets it Toxic a Steel or Poison type that believes it is immune, which is the answer to the walls this team cannot break; its Fake Out supports Darkrai's Nasty Plot or a risk-bearing Hypnosis. Reserves & disruption: Meowscarada's Protean changes its type to match each move, and Flower Trick is a Grass attack that always lands and always critically hits - it ignores accuracy checks, evasion, Focus Sash-preserving defence boosts and Reflect entirely. Bad Dreams damages any sleeping opponent each turn, so Hypnosis and Bad Dreams reinforce each other, but Hypnosis is never a guaranteed setup window and must not be scored as one. Could this team be cooler? Yes, and one slot changed. Overqwil was this roster's third appearance in the audit range and did nothing the team needed; Meowscarada replaces it with a genuinely rare starter whose Flower Trick is the single most reliable attack in the range - a guaranteed critical hit that no defensive boost, screen or evasion can stop - which pairs with Queenly Majesty to make this a fight about being unable to defend rather than unable to attack. The Mega Darkrai remains the draw and the honest limitation stays recorded: its base ability may not survive transformation. Overrepresented? primary_question: Can the player beat this elite team (Kyogre, Tornadus Therian, Zapdos, Lugia, Terapagos, Mewtwo) on its own terms: Concept: the Champion off duty, with no type restriction and no reason to hold back - a primal storm with five legends standing in it. First two useful turns: Kyogre's Drizzle is live on entry and its Mystic Water raises Origin Pulse further; Thunder never misses in that rain, which is why the whole roster is built around electricity and wind. Therian Tornadus sets Tailwind when the speed race matters or fires Bleakwind Storm, which is perfectly accurate in rain and lowers the Speed of both targets it hits. Turn two makes a real Regenerator switch only when the replacement improves the board - Tornadus refunds a third of its HP on the way out. Alternate deployment: Zapdos is the second rain abuser and the fight's most punishing body - Thunder at full accuracy and Hurricane at full accuracy from a Pokemon with no Ground weakness through the storm. Lugia's Multiscale halves every hit while it is at full HP, and Calm Mind behind that bulk makes it the win condition a player cannot out-stall. Reserves & disruption: Terapagos awakens the moment it enters - its custom Terra ability swaps it into its crystal form for that form's bulk and offence, with no item, charge or player-side counterpart, and Tri Attack is the same-turn STAB that punishes anything that stays in to trade. Mega Mewtwo X is the physical closer in an otherwise entirely special roster, which is the point: the defensive answer the player has been building all fight is the wrong one. Could this team be cooler? It is cooler now, and the change was about making the storm mean something. The authored roster carried an Arceus with no plate - an ordinary Normal type wearing the most famous name in the series - and a base Calyrex whose Helping Hand support was far below the tier of everything around it. Replacing them with Zapdos and Lugia turns a list of famous names into a team: Zapdos converts the rain into guaranteed 110-power attacks, and Lugia is the wall that makes the fight last long enough for that to matter. Every remaining member now either makes the weather, uses the weather, or deliberately ignores it. Overrepresented? Kyogre is shared with Champion Wallace's own League team by design - this is the same trainer showing the same partner without the type restriction - and Tornadus, Zapdos, Lugia, Terapagos and Mega Mewtwo X appear nowhere else in the campaign. Mewtwo's other form, Y, belongs to Leaf's optional fight, which is a deliberate pairing. Levels: cap 100, offsets 2/2/2/2/2/3. This is optional post-game content and is meant to be the hardest fight in the game.
theme_and_tempo: Concept: the Champion off duty, with no type restriction and no reason to hold back - a primal storm with five legends standing in it. primary_question: Can the player beat this rival team (Ninetales, Kangaskhan, Gengar, Tangrowth, Snorlax, Mewtwo) on its own terms: Concept: the Kanto challenger in Altering Cave - six Pokemon from a different region's memory, led by sun and ended by the strongest Psychic attacker in the series. First two useful turns: Ninetales establishes Drought on entry, so Solar Beam needs no charge turn and Encore can lock a wasted opposing action; Kangaskhan opens with Fake Out or immediate Scrappy pressure, which lets its Normal attacks hit Ghost types that would otherwise be immune. Turn two pivots to whichever support and threat pair the opening revealed. Alternate deployment: Chlorophyll Tangrowth is already at doubled Speed in its own sun and uses Rage Powder to hold the field for Mega Mewtwo Y's special offence, or Sleep Powder to remove a threat outright. Reserves & disruption: Gengar supplies Icy Wind speed control and Sludge Bomb, and Snorlax is the immovable object - Thick Fat halves incoming Fire and Ice damage, Recycle restores its consumed Leftovers, and its HP is large enough to absorb the burst the player was saving for Mewtwo. Rage Powder has ordinary target restrictions and cannot protect against spread attacks. Could this team be cooler? Yes, and one slot changed for both theme and duplication. Zeraora is not a Kanto Pokemon and it duplicated Vincent's Mega two doors earlier, so it was doing double damage to the fight's identity. Snorlax replaces it with the most recognisable Kanto body in the series, gives the roster the physical wall it completely lacked, and adds a genuinely memorable interaction in Recycle - a Snorlax that keeps eating its own Leftovers is a wall the player has to actually kill rather than outlast. The team now reads as exactly what it is: a Kanto champion's party, unchanged in spirit, ending on Mega Mewtwo Y. Overrepresented? Snorlax, Kangaskhan's base Scrappy set, Tangrowth and Mega Mewtwo Y are unique in the campaign; Ninetales's Drought recurs with Vito and the Magma arc at lower tiers; Gengar's other owners are the route ace Mollie and Phoebe's League Mega, all with different items and roles. Levels: cap 100, offsets 1/1/1/1/1/2, scaled to the live cap rather than the discarded fixed level-100 floor.

primary_question: Can the player beat this rival team (Skarmory, Rayquaza, Cradily, Melmetal, Dialga, Metagross) on its own terms: Concept: the Steel champion's exhibition team - a steel spine, a fossil support, and two of Hoenn's and Sinnoh's heaviest legends, with exactly one Mega between them. First two useful turns: Skarmory chooses Tailwind only when Rayquaza's attack or a safe Dragon Dance actually benefits, and Body Press otherwise, converting its own enormous Defence into damage behind Sturdy; Rayquaza attacks, with Air Lock suppressing every weather effect on the field for as long as it is out - which quietly turns off a player's rain, sun or sand team without spending a move. Turn two attacks through the speed window or brings the appropriate heavy reserve. Alternate deployment: Cradily's Storm Drain draws opposing single-target Water attacks away from Melmetal and converts them into a Special Attack boost, and Melmetal's Double Iron Bash hits twice with a flinch chance on each hit, which the Iron Fist ability boosts further. Reserves & disruption: Dialga is the special coverage lane with Pressure doubling the PP cost of every move aimed at it. The Mega designation belongs to Metagross alone - Rayquaza's move-based eligibility must never be allowed to create a second transformation for the same trainer, and the team is built assuming Rayquaza stays untransformed. Steven's fixed allied party in the Mossdeep multi battle is a separate roster and must never be replaced with this exhibition team. Could this team be cooler? The composition is right and stays: Air Lock as free weather suppression, Storm Drain protecting a Steel giant from its worst matchup, and a Mega Metagross closer is a legible, characterful Steven team, and the restraint of one Mega among two legends is what keeps it from being a list. What the block needed was the amendment made explicit rather than pending - Metagross is now the designated Mega in both prose and slot - plus post-game level offsets so the exhibition is a real fight. Overrepresented? Skarmory, Rayquaza, Cradily, Melmetal and Dialga are unique in the campaign; Mega Metagross recurs in the earlier Magma and multi-battle blocks, which is correct - it is Steven's signature and the player has seen it fighting alongside them before meeting it across the field. === ENCOUNTER 0513 ===
physical_group_id: PHYSICAL_MOSSDEEPCITY_HOUSE1_0033
proposed_encounter_id: PHYSICAL_MOSSDEEPCITY_HOUSE1_0033
campaign_order: 513
atlas_ordinal: 513
chapter: Postgame
strict_cap: 100
location: MossdeepCity_House1
requirement: optional
status: master_audited_ready_for_implementation
battle_class: leader
ai_profile: master
primary_question: Can the player beat this leader team (Milotic, Togekiss, Spiritomb, Lucario, Miraidon, Garchomp) on its own terms: Concept: the last fight in the campaign. Cynthia brings her own team - the Sinnoh partners the player will recognise on sight - with one future-paradox legend and a custom Mega Garchomp to finish. First two useful turns: Togekiss uses Follow Me to pull a single-target attack away from Spiritomb or Lucario, or Air Slash, whose flinch chance Serene Grace doubles to 60% - the highest-value single click on the board; Milotic attacks or recovers, and Competitive doubles its Special Attack the moment any stat of its is lowered, so an Intimidate or a Snarl aimed at her lead hands her the fight. Turn two brings a real attacker rather than repeating the support. Alternate deployment: Togekiss supports Miraidon's special pressure after the deliberate Electric Terrain transition - Hadron Engine sets the terrain on entry and raises Miraidon's own Special Attack by a third while it is up, and Electro Drift does extra damage against anything it is super effective against. Reserves & disruption: Spiritomb has no type weaknesses at all and its Infiltrator ignores screens and Substitutes; mixed Choice Scarf Lucario is the surprise speed tier, capable of both Close Combat and Aura Sphere; Mega Garchomp Z is a custom form whose stats and ability must be read from source rather than imported from the ordinary Mega. Note that Electric Terrain prevents grounded Pokemon from falling asleep, which is exactly why this team carries no sleep move - the terrain phase and the support phase do not fight each other. Could this team be cooler? It is cooler now for one specific reason. The authored version paired Roserade's Sleep Powder with Miraidon's Electric Terrain, which makes that Sleep Powder fail against every grounded target on the field - the team's own ace disabled its own lead, and the block could only flag the conflict rather than fix it. Replacing Roserade with Milotic resolves it completely, restores one of Cynthia's most recognisable partners, and swaps a fragile sleep gamble for a Competitive trap that punishes the Intimidate and Snarl leads a player brings to a physical-looking team. The result is a final boss whose six members are all hers and whose two phases no longer contradict. Overrepresented? Spiritomb, Lucario, Miraidon and Mega Garchomp Z are unique in the campaign; Togekiss is Cynthia's alone now that Wally is rebuilt around his own partners; Milotic's other owner is Champion Wallace's Mega, which is the right contrast - the Champion's Milotic is a Mega wall, hers is a Competitive attacker; Garchomp's other owner is Caroline's sand team in Victory Road. Levels: cap 100, offsets 2/2/3/3/3/4 - the highest-level opponents in the game, and deliberately so.
